Hon. A. K. MACLEAN (Acting Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 62, to amend the Insurance Act, 1917.
Explain.

The purpose of this Bill is threefold. The Insurance Act now provides that British and foreign companies shall maintain a deposit with the Department of Finance at least equal to their total liabilities in Canada. The pur-

pose of this Bill is to require that the deposit shall not only equal the amount of their liabilities in Canada, but shall be in excess of their liabilities to the extent of 25 per cent. The second amendment proposed is to increase the initial deposit required of British and foreign companies prior to the commencement of their insurance business in Canada. The amount required to-day is $50,000, and it is proposed to raise that to $100,000. The third amendment proposed is to section 125 of the Insurance Act, which requires Canadian companies to maintain assets at least 15 per cent in excess of their total liabilities. The Bill proposes to raise the amount of this percentage to 25 per cent.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.
Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 63, to amend the Fisheries Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This Bill is introduced for two specific reasons. The first provision refers to the British Columbia salmon fisheries. Heretofore it has been the custom to have the packages or cases labelled to show that the salmon was caught legally, or that the salmon was caught during the open season and not during the closed season. The department has found that this provision of the law has not worked out as satisfactorily as was hoped, and the object of the Bill is to abolish clauses 22, 23, 25, 65 and 66, as a result of which no one will be allowed to catch fish outside of the areas that are closed during the closed season unless he has a license, or unless the boat is licensed. The Indians have a habit, during the closed fishing season, of catching a considerable number of salmon. While they are allowed legally to catch salmon for their own use, they are *forbidden to catch salmon and offer them for sale either to the canners or the dealers. The object is to prevent any one offering salmon during the close season to any canner or dealer, unless either the boat or the man is licensed.
During the cloee season in Canadian waters it has been the practice of some of the Canadian lobster fishermen, and also of some of the American lobster fishermen, to catch lobsters outside of the territorial waters. It is proposed' by this legislation, concurrent legislation being passed by the United States Congress, to prevent the Canadian and American fishermen from

catching lobsters during the close season outside of the territorial waters.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

When the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn) was speaking on this subject some few days ago, I had not the honour of being present while he was taking up the -question of the disbandonment of the 5th Division. In the year 1916, in order to get the Canadian forces properly organized with a view to meeting conditions that we expected to-arise in the future, and that have since materialized, I drew up a memorandum recommending to General Sir Douglas Haig, General Sir William Robertson and Mr. Lloyd George-and I sent a copy of it to the Prime Minister of Canada-that Canada, to have a perfect force, should have two army corps each consisting of three divisions. The usual British army corps is made up of two divisions, each division being made up of four brigades, with odd battalions for pioneer and other purposes, and from time to time various additions to that have been made in the way of machine gun sections- and so forth. Each brigade is made up^of four battalions, each numbering 1,000 men. The British force had not at that time, as the Minister of Militia very properly stated, maintained any fixed standard, but two divisions constituted an army corps. Following that rule, Canada, from the moment we had four divisions organized, should have had two army corps in the field. I submitted my plan and I discussed it with Sir Douglas Haig, Sir William Robertson and all the leading officers. My idea was that we would hold, with six div-

isions or two army corps, no more trenches than we did with one army corps or four divisions. Our frontage would be exactly the same, and consequently our losses would be neither more nor less than they are now. In order, however, that the men might get- proper rest, my scheme was that we should have one division in the front trenches, one division in support and one division in reserve, resting. I made plans for six divisions, constituting two army corps. My plan met with the approval of Sir Douglas Haig, Sir William Robertson, Mr. Lloyd George and every officer in Europe whom I consulted and whose opinion was worth anything. In fact, my scheme met with so much approval that six or seven or eight months afterwards the German army was remodelled on the identical system that I had the honour of devising beforehand. Later on, the British army, always conservative and slow in the way of taking up anything new, adopted a similar principle, and to-day the principle generally adopted in the British army is to have three divisions constituting an army corps. I shall not enter into the details of the composition of the army corps, but the standard which I had set was not lived up to. I had also planned that in addition to the men in the three divisions in each corps each battalion should have men in rest, and that at Havre we should have a camp prepared for reinforcements which we could send hither and thither as the need might become urgent. I merely point this out to show to the House and the country that the statements made here that the British' army has not adopted the principle of three divisions to a corps and that the German army has not adopted it, are not in accordance with the facts. I do not hold any body here responsible for that because the statements come from the other side. I devised my scheme early in 1916, and the boys would have been much better off if it had been adopted. It would not have taken one man more than the present system because the area held by our forces would not have been any greater. If my scheme had been carried out, we would not have had some of the massacres that we have had at the front. I do not think anybody overseas in the Canadian service considered the matter sufficiently to be able to give an intelligent opinion as to what was really needed, or we certainly should have had two army corps instead of one.
Would that imply a reorganization of the present system?

There are now four divisions. In 1916 I had four divisions in the field and two additional divisions, in all six, all ready to form into two army corps. The scheme was held up on my retirement, but I am in a position to say without fear of contradiction that with the exception of the first division, which was the best, shooting division in the world, the fifth division was the best trained in the world. Upwards of six to eight hundred men in every battalion had received sufficient training to handle a machine gun section, and about eight hundred out of every thousand men were instructors. There were plenty of men to form another division. If that had been done we would have had two corps instead of one, and at the same, time we would have had no more frontage to look after-no more men exposed to fire than now-but there would always have been one division in each corps in rest billets. Let me again emphasize that 1 submitted this proposal to Sir Douglas Haig and the British War Office and received their approval. The Germans have adopted the same system; it is only common sense to have one division in attack, one in support, and one in rest all the time. I had also plans for having a couple of hundred men in each battalion right at hand to fill up gaps, and then there was the training camp at Havre. All these plans have since been carried out in detail with the exception of forming the two corps. The British are also adopting the system of having three divisions to a corps. I want this to be made clear. The statement furnished by the Minister of Militia and Defence is not in accordance with the facts, so far as the British army is concerned, because they have already adopted the policy of three divisions to a corps.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course, we would be venturing upon very dangerous ground if we should undertake to overrule the commander of the Canadian army 'corps in regard to matters of that kind. There was only one question that I found it necessary to take up with the British authorities when I was in England a year ago, and I took it up with Sir Douglas Haig, with the Secretary of State for War, Lord Derby, and with Mr. Lloyd George himself. I came to the conclusion while I was over there, after conferences with General Currie and General Turner, that the divisional and corps staffs did not have in their personnel a sufficient proportion of Canadians.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We had men who, in the course of a year and a half or two years experience, had obtained or could have obtained the training which would qualify them for important staff positions. More than that, we had men who, while they were not perhaps qualified to take the higher positions on the staff, might very well have been appointed to junior positions on the divisional staff or corps staff, and in that way might have fitted them-

selves 'for taking higher staff positions. The representations which I made to Sir Douglas Haig, the Secretary of State for War, and the Prime Minister, had effect, as I was informed subsequently, and I believe that in consequence Canadians are now represented much more fully than formerly upon the divisional and corps staffs.
Hear, hear.

In regard to the Canadian force, a question which I desire to ask the Minister of Militia and Defence from curiosity, was stimulated by an article that appeared in the press some little time ago as coming from Ottawa. The article appeared at the time certain representatives of the "Originals," as they were called, the First Contingent, return to Canada. The question under discussion in the article was as to whether or not the power was vested in the Canadian Government to give these men, who had been granted a furlough, a further furlough in Canada, if that was desired. The despatch from Ottawa read:
The Government is not likely to vary the conditions under which furlough was secured for men of the First Division. Resolutions, and also letters from individuals, are being sent here inquiring that as these brave men have done their bit and stood the brunt of very hard service for over three years, they should be allowed to remain at home.
It is conceded that in many cases, sending them back involves real hardship, but when the announcement was made that they were coming it was accompanied' by a warning that they would have to return to service.
It was stated that this was a specific agreement with the British authorities, on the strength of which the respite was secured. If it is broken, then the department says it will be a case of good-bye to leaves of absence for other contingents. A hundred men who had their furlough have already gone back.
An exception is likely to be made in the case of men who are physically unfit. In such cases, the weeding out will probably be done in Canada, rather than on the return to England.
It is the agreement with the British authorities stipulating that the men were to return to service that now is particularly cited as a reason why the repeated applications for discharge cannot be granted.
That despatch would seem to lead one to the conclusion that the Government admitted that they had no authority to withdraw from Europe to Canada any men of the Canadian contingent without the consent of the British Government. II do not want to take a too narrow or academic view of this question but it would seem to suggest the question as to what the position of Canada in this war is. I always had the idea that in this war we occupied a different position from that which Canada has
occupied in any other war. In the South African war we allowed-our men to go but the British Government paid the bill and, they paying the bill, the contractual relation between the soldier and the British Government probably gave them the right to insist upon the retention of any man. But in this war, we are paying the bill. We are paying not only the wages of the soldier but we are paying for his maintenance and equipment in the field. True all the equipment is not being supplied directly from Canada. Some equipment is being supplied by Britain on our account, but the disbursement is being charged against us.
Now to put it briefly, and perhaps epi-grammatically, the point I want to insist on ie this:	that we are there as allies
and not as vassals. I think the Canadian Government should make it perfectly clear to the Canadian people that our men in Europe are under our control, not in relation to matters of promotion, because I quite agree with what the Prime Minister says that it would be ridiculous from three thousand miles away for us to endeavour to determine.who should have promotion, but surely our men are under our control to this extent-that if there should be a disaster, or something should occur that the Canadian Government thought occurred from mismanagement abroad, we, as a Canadian Parliament, would have the right to ask the Canadian Government for an explanation, and the Government would 'be obliged to lay that explanation on the Table of this House.
Sir StAiM HUGHES: Hear, hear.

And I resent a little the position that apparently has been taken, if the memorandum which I have just read is correct, because it seems to imply that we have no fullness of control over the* Canadian army. That I think the Government should insist upon, and I believe the Canadian people will support them in that insistence.
Major-General MEWBURN: In reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Kingston regarding the furlough granted to some men of the First Canadian Contingent, I might say that the matter was taken up last summer to see if some of the men could be brought back. Again last fall, after Sir Edward Kemp went to England, there was some correspondence on the subject. Negotiations went on for some time, and we finally, after a great deal of effort, arranged to get the married men of the

First Contingent, who had families in Canada, three .months furlough in this country. The Australian and New Zealand Governments endeavoured to make the same arrangement, but were not successful. These men were given three months furlough to Canada on the understanding, as any soldier who is granted a furlough knows, that it is his duty as a soldier to return when that furlough expires.

With whom was that arrangement made?
Major-General MEWBURN: The arrangement was made, starting with the Overseas Minister of Militia in London, England. It was taken up by the corps commander in France, and everybody knows that that officer is the supreme authority in the field over the men under him. General Currie took the matter into consideration, and it became a question whether he could afford to allow all these men to leave the front in view of the difficulty of replacing them by experienced soldiers. The idea was that when the first soldiers who had been granted furlough returned, additional men would be given the privilege; it was simply a matter of keeping faith with the men that were left at the front in the hope that it would be possible for them to enjoy a simitar furlough. The War Office had nothing whatever to do with the matter,; it was a question, for the corps commander of the whole British force, of which the Canadian corps is an integral part, to deal with. Well, the condition was as I have described; it was a case to be dealt with by Sir Douglas Haig, who was Commander in Chief of the British forces in France, including not only the British army but the military forces from the Overseas Dominions-what we look upon as the British army. The forces are entirely under Field Marshal Haig's control; he has the right to say whether a man can be allowed to go on furlough, or be given any other privilege, and his power is absolute.

Who is the army commander over the Canadians to-day?
Major-General MEWBURN: Do you mean since General Byng left? Our men are directly under General Currie.

General Currie is only the corps commander, who is- the army commander?
Major-General MEWBURN: I could net state offhand. However, to continue, these men did get leave, and it has been a very big problem to know exactly what to do in the matter. My hon. friend from
fMajor-General Mewburn.]
Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) knows of the [DOT] large number of men that were biought back from the front since 1914, -officers on leave, and men on furlough [DOT] whose leave or furlough was extended from time to time, and of others who were permitted to remain in Canada. In this particular instance it is a very great hardship when these men come out here, these married men, to force them to go ibaek at the expiration of their furlough, but I am glad to say there have been very few cases of men refusing to go back. When these men return to England before their furlough has expired, under our new organization, they are taken into one of the depot battalions in the district to which they go until the expiration of their furlough. A large number of the men of the First Contingent have returned to England before their furlough was up. In fact one of our good soldiers from the Emerald Isle, who went back before his furlough was up, when asked why he went back before he had to go, said he had been in a good many fights in which there was always a policeman to stop him, but in this case there was no policeman, and he desired to get back before the fighting was over. No doubt this is the view of a good many of our men. The Government, of course, has power to say whether these men of the First Contingent shall be discharged, or whether they shall remain and continue on military duty in Canada. We can take that action if we so desire. It is not a question of any action by the War Office, -who have nothing to do with it; it is a matter of keeping faith with the men still at the front, and of having those who received a furlough go back when that furlough expires.

The question I asked was who was responsible for ordering Colonel Martin back from the front, and by whose authority did he return from the front? Mr. COCKSHUTT We are voting a large sum of money for war purposes. I do not know where it is coming from but I assume it will be raised by loans. What I am especially interested in, however, is how this money is to be paid out. I represent a constituency that has sent a good many men to the front, and a great many cases of deferred payments have been brought to my attention. I assume that every member of the House has had the same experience. The matter of assigned pay and separation allowance may seem to be one of detail as compared with the large question of the management of our armies, but it is very important that the wives and mothers of the boys who have gone overseas should receive these payments promptly. There would appear to be too much delay in the distribution of assigned pay and separation allowance. I am not holding the minister responsible; he no doubt is making the best of a difficult situation. But I know of many cases in which payments have been delayed three, four, even six months, and I do think that an effort should be made to distribute this money more promptly. The assurance is always given: " the Government of Canada owes you this money, so you will be sure to get it." But that does not pay grocery bills or other liabilities that may accumulate. Moreover, that spirit is altogether too evident in matters dealt with by departments of the Government generally. My idea is that payments made by the Government should be just as promptly attended to as are collections for Government purposes. If the Customs and Inland Revenue Departments demand cash on the spot for goods received, the Government should exercise the same principle in making payments; they should discharge their obligation juet as promptly as the individual is expected to discharge his to the Government. There is a tendency in many of the departments-the Militia is not the only offender in- this respect-to delay payments unduly, and many private individuals suffer from time to time as a result. I speak on behalf of the returned soldiers, men ' 
who are wounded, men who are depending upon their military pay, when I urge that the payments to which I have referred be expedited to the greatest possible extent; that they be distributed whenever they fall <fue. I have no doubt the minister can assure me that improvement will be effected in the near future, as improvement is being made even now to a certain extent.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I not only
say it will be improved, (but I can honestly say that it has been improved 90 per cent during the last two or three months. I made a statement in the House about a week ago with regard to the assigned pay and separation allowance branch, which pays out about $5,000,000 a month in separation allowance and assigned pay. I do not take credit for the improvement that has been effected; I want to give credit where credit is due. There has been a great deal of difficulty in that- branch; many -mistakes were made

there is no use denying it. But I can also say that during the last two or three months there have been very few complaints that the women have not received their cheques promptly.
The officer whom I have in charge there, Major Stiff, at my earnest solicitation, took that position temporarily, so that^he might [DOT]re-organize the department. He-is anxious to get back to his own business. He has been overseas. He is a man of the highest standard in accounting and in business generally. He has surrounded himself with efficient help, and if any hon. gentleman in this House could spare ten or fifteen minutes, or even half an hour, to go through the offices of the separation allowance and assigned pay branch with Major Stiff, it would be an object lesson to him to see what has been and is being accomplished and the enormous quantity of work that is being done. I would appreciate it if any hon. gentleman would take the trouble to go through those offices, because hon. gentlemen receive letters from many of their constituents who have soldier relatives overseas, and we welcome any information in regard to delays. We are there for the purpose of straightening out any complaints. That branch has a big responsibility, as have many others, and I believe if any hon. gentleman would go through it with Major Stiff, he would get an eye opener.

Yesterday, I had occasion to go down to the separation allowance and assigned pay office on behalf of a lady who lives in-the northern part of my constituency and who had not received

her separation allowance cheque for over two months. The probable reason for the delay in her case is that when a soldier*, goes overseas, separation allowance cheques are paid from the Ottawa office, and when the soldier returns from overseas the cheques are paid from the military district in which he is located. I have on two or three occasions visited the separation allowance and assigned pay office, and I have been very greatly impressed, not only with the enormous quantity of work which is being carried on there, but with the earnestness and efficiency evidenced. Yesterday morning, when I called at the office,
I failed to obtain an interview With Major Stiff. His assistant was not in at the time, but a young lady stepped up to the counter. I told her what I wanted, showing her the letter I had received from this person in my constituency, and she took hold of the matter in a very businesslike way. She was a very bright and intelligent young lady. In the afternoon I received a communication from the office showing that they had taken vigorous steps to have the matter rectified.
In regard to this vast amount of money and how it is to be expended, I want to mention just one case as an illustration of the way in which I think money for military purposes is not being properly expended, or is, in a sense, being misappropriated. In the Department of Justice there is an official who acts as purchasing agent for the penitentiaries, and who has been receiving for that work a salary of $3,300 a year. From all I can learn, I believe he is quite an efficient man. I understand, however, that in addition to acting as purchasing agent- for the penitentiaries, he was required to act as purchasing agent for the internment camps.
Where is that officer?

I do not know where he is-somewhere in Canada, I presume. His name is Dillon, and he is purchasing agent for 'the penitentiaries. I presume his head office is in the city of Ottawa; I do not know the street number. The hon. member can get the information by applying to headquarters. I do not know that the work of purchasing supplies for the internment campis added very materially to his other work, but if it did, it seems to me the proper way to deal with the matter would be for the Government to inform the House, and if this gentleman is not receiving as large a salary as he should receive, then his salafy should be increased. Instead of that course being pursued, the very roundabout method was adopted of saying: This can be very easily fixed; we want to increase your salary; we shall simply make you a captain and give you a captain's pay. His salary was boosted from $3,300 to over $5,000 by the simple expedient of making him a captain.
Captain of what?
Captain of the Lord knows what, I do not know what.
He must be the only captain who draws as much pay as that. I can assure my hon. friend a captain's pay is not as large as that.
Is it not eighteen hundred and some odd dollars?
Perhaps he is an honorary captain.

If he holds the rank of honorary captain, one thing is quite certain, that if my hon. friend had been Minister of Militia at the time, Mr. Dillon would not have been given that rank; he would have been made an honorary colonel. My hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) was in the habit of making one, batch of honorary colonels before breakfast and if his food agreed with him, another batch after breakfast.
I was very particular in the matter of selecting men for the rank of honorary colonel.

I cannot agree with
my hon. friend in that respect. There are many military matters in which I do not think my hon. friend has been particular, and not only in regard to appointing honorary colonels but also some who were neither honorary nor honored. Nevertheless, he was one of the colonels who retained bis rank all the time my hon, friend (Sir Sam Hughes) held the office of Minister of Militia.

Might I rise to a question of privilege? Armand Lavergne was not a colonel all the time that I was

minister. He took his training, and then I made him a colonel. I did not make him an honorary colonel. Some reference has been made by my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) to interference in the handling of men overseas. I would ask those hon. gentlemen who are a little scared that this blessed autonomy of ours which so frequently crops up will be interfered with by something or other done over the water: what in Heaven's name has Great Britain ever done that we cannot trust her? When has she ever tried to put the shackles on this country, that some person is always getting up and saying we must keep the power in our own hands and not let the control be over there. Such a declaration always brings a round of applause from some hon. gentlemen, particularly from those on the other side of the House, who have never distinguished themselves by doing anything for Great Britain or Canada. That is the situation. What have the officers in this country connected with our militia ever done to make us think we could better rely on their judgment than on the judgment of the men who are handling the situation overseas? What has my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) ever done in the past that we should take his opinion on matters overseas, 5 p.m. in preference to the opinion of the men handling the situation over there? Where has he buried hie dead? Where is his private cemetery? If we had a man in Canada, including my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton, big enough in a military sense to go overseas and make his bigness felt, not only England but every one of the Allied nations would be only too glad to place him jn supreme command, and the men of England and the men of France would take their orders from him without any fear of losing their autonomy. I am sick and tired of this cheeseparing in regard to what they do over in England and at the front in regard to our Canadian troops. England and France appreciate every effort that has been made by this country in the war, and they . have no idea other than to be absolutely fair and just to the men who left our shores to help them in the fight. And it ill becomes us in this House to say anything which in the least savours of a reflection upon those across the water who (have-charge of the conduct of this war, and especially in connection with their treatment of our Canadian troops.

To revert to the subject
of the returned soldier, I know a number, in fact, virtually all, of the married men remaining of the First Division who are home on furlough; there are about 800 of them altogether. These men who have served in the trenches for over three years have been allowed to come back and see their wives and children, but I understand in a number of cases the ships they came over on were delayed in England on account of submarines to such an extent that some of the men have only had a week at home. I would appeal to the minister to extend the leave of all these men in this country by thirty days, and also to-give them a medical board before they go back, so that we shall be sure we are not sending cripples to the front. They should at least 'be allowed a full month at home with their wives and families. There are not so many of them that it wmuld cause any great difficulty. I know I am asking this in the face of a great battle in which our men may become engaged, but I understand a number of these returned men were in Irllets in England for a few days or weeks before they left. So I think I might ask the minister to soften his heart a little, and if he does, I .am sure the cause of the allies will not suffer, because every one of these men has his heart in the war and is anxious to go back. I think it is only fair they should be given the full leave they have been deprived of by the submarine menace.
Major - General MEWBURN Arrangements have already been made for giving these men a medical board before returning, and an effort has already been made to have extended the furlough of those who were delayed in coming across.

The other evening I promised that when the militia estimates were under consideration I would make a statement as to the duties of the Director of Public Information and the work he is carrying on. As his salary will be paid out of the war appropriation, this is probably a suitable time to make the statement. The work of the Director of Public Information, on the limited scale applicable to Canada, is similar in character to that being carried on by the Bureau of Public Information in the United States, and to the Ministry of Information in Great Britain. As the hon. members of the House are aware, in all the countries at war there are departments that deal with dissemination of information relating to the war among their own people, as well as blanches of the service dealing with propaganda abroad, and the idea back of the creation of this directorship of public information in Canada was exactly the same.
If we are to sustain the spirit of the people; if through the long and trying years of this struggle we are to retain their continued interest and enthusiasm in supporting the war effort of the country, we must endeavour to supply them with the fullest possible information in connection with the conduct of the war. One of the primary objects in creating this branch of the public service was to supply still fuller information to the people of Canada in reference tc the progress of the war and Canada's participation in it. There has also been placed under the charge of the Director of Public Information the publication of the Canadian Daily Record for our troops overseas. This paper is edited and conducted by returned officers who have served at the front.
Who is the head of this department?
Mr. Nichols.
Late of the Montreal Daily Mail?
Yes. Capt. Wallace is in actual charge of the publication of the Daily Record.
Not our hon. friend from West York?

No, he is a newspaper
man who has served overseas and is now back in Canada. The information is cabled over and the Daily Record is published for the information of the men in the trenches. News which would interest the men at the front is being supplied every day. I am informed that in so far as the supplying of home nows is concerned., the Daily Record is recognized as being the best publication going to any of the troops overseas, The arrangements for the publication of the Daily Record and its supervision were placed under the direction of, the Director of Public Information in January or February of this year. I am sure the members of the House will all agree that it is a wise thing that the men overseas should be kept in touch with what is going on in Canada, that they should have the news from Canada and that the home ties should be maintained through such a publication.

How many words
are sent daily?
From 1,000 to 1,500 words of the general news, of Canada are cabled daily.	.

Is this the Record
from which were omitted the names of certain soldiers who were candidates in the last election?

I have no knowledge of
that matter. The supervision of the Record came under the charge of the Director of Public Information in January or February of the present year, some time after the election, and 1 have no knowledge of conditions prior to that time. The paper is printed in London and is despatched to the soldiers overseas. I suppose most of the members have seen this paper; it is a small publication of four pagesr. The Director of Public Information ie also responsible for seeing that news which the Government receives in connection with the war and which can properly be made public reaches the press of the country.
Mr. ROSiS: I understand that this Record was published before January. Under whose charge was it published before that time?

The news was being supplied by officers of the militia; I presume under the Militia Department. It was published in London, the information being sent from Canada. In addition, the Director of Public Information is responsible for seeing that news of important decisions of the Government, particularly relating to the war, reaches the public press. In the ordinary course, information as to the important acts of the Government, in the great majority of cases, is communicated direct to the press either by the Prime Minister or the ministers in Charge of the different departments. But, it is the duty of the Director of Public Information to keep in touch with the various departments and tp see that their important acts are communicated to the press. One of the difficulties of aJll ministers, and of departmental officers, is that there as such a pressure upon their time and attention, especially during a period of stress like this, that not sufficient attention is given to communicating to the public news of importance. The public is entitled to the fullest possible information as to what is being done by the Government, in order that it may be kept in touch with the situation. That is an important phase of the work which must be developed as time goes on.

Are the advertisements which appear in the Record paid for?
flMr. Rowel 1. ]
I cannot say as to that. It is published in England. All we are responsible for here is sending over the news. .

Are you responsible for the advertisements published in it? For a period of about three weeks previous to the election, the Daily Record was plastered with advertisements asking the soldiers to vote against the friends of the Kaiser. Were these paid for, and, if so, by whom?
The Record was not under the control of the Director of Public Information at that time, and I have no knowledge of the matters to which my hon. friend 'has referred.
Under whose control was it?
It was published in England.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Power) if he has, any objection to the advertisement to which he has referred?

I have an objection to the manner in which the words were uised, and I have a grave1 objection to pointing out the people on this side of the House as being friends of the Kaiser. I have, as well, a particular objection to the members of the Government, who were candidates at that time, treating their opponents as such.

Is there a complete file of that publication in the reading room of the House? If not, I think it would be wise to keep a complete file of the paper so that it would be available for reference, and so that we could check up the matters appearing an it.

I will make inquiries as to the point about which the hon. gentleman asks. I do not know whether there is a file or not. I have no doubt there is a file in the department of the publication since .it came under the charge of the Director of Public Information.
I propose now to speak of the propaganda wmk of the Director of Public Information. The members of the House would not expect me to go into matters of detail in connection with the question of propaganda outside our own country. Yet, I am sure, they will recognize that there are coadi-tions under which it might be desirable that Canada's war efforts, and what we are doing in this country, should be made known outside of Canada. We are one of the allied nations and it is important that

the facts in connection with our participation in the war should be kept before other peoples as well as our own. That is becoming increasingly important in connection with our relations with our neighbours to the south. This is a matter which comes under the charge of the Director of Public Information. He is in touch with the American Committee of Public Information and they are rendering help and assistance to each other. He is also in touch with the British 'Ministry of Information and arrangements have been made for co-operation between the British Ministry of Information and the Director of Public Information here. They are placing at our disposal much of the literature which has been published there insofar as we desire to use it in Canada. Many pamphlets, of very great value, dealing with certain war conditions in Europe have been placed at our disposal for use and distribution in Canada. That arrangement was made only recently.
There is another aspect of the work of the department to which I would like to draw attention and that is what is known 'as the War Lecture Bureau, or what might be described as oral propaganda. I am sure we realize the invaluable service which the press of Canada has rendered during this war in placing before the people of Canada the facts in connection with the war and in sustaining the spirit of the people during the whole course of the struggle.
Is it in recognition of the splendid services of the press of this country in stimulating recruiting that hundreds of dollars have been paid out to Le Devoir for Government advertising?

The advertisements that have been printed in the newspaper to which my hon. friend refers do not come under the cognizance of my department, and, therefore, I cannot give my hon. friend the information he desires.
I was going on to .say that we all recognize the value of the press, but nothing will fully take the place of the oral appeal, the living voice in appeal, to the people in connection with the war, and in communicating to them the facts bearing on the war. That has been one of the most important developments in the work of the Bureau of Public Information in the United States, and of the Ministry of Information in Great Britain. In both those countries they have organized volunteer speakers, who discuss the varying issues and phases of the war before the people in order that the whole
nation may, so far as is practicable, be kept in the most vital touch, not only with the war situation, but with the efforts of the nation itself in the prosecution of the war.
What is the personnel of the Bureau?

It consists of a travelling secretary, who is organizing these voluntary groups or associations in the various cities and towns. The workers are all volunteers throughout the cities, towns and rural sections of Canada. There is also an official who assists in the office with the work of this bureau, as weE as with the press work.

What are the names of the officers who assist in the work here?
I may as well confess that I am suspicious of the entire outfit.
I cannot help my hon. friend's suspicions; I can only state the . facts.
I would like to get their names.

Mr. Frank Yeigh, of Toronto, is the organizing secretary of the War Lecture Bureau throughout the country, and Mr. LeSueur is .associated with Mr. Nichols in the office. He assists not only in the work of the War Lecture Bureau, but also in the work for the press.
Is he a son of the former secretary of the Post Office Department, the late Mr. LeSueur?
I do not know the position of Mr. LeSueur's father, but this gentleman was identified with Y.M.C.A. work before he entered upon his present duties.
I think he is the son of the late Mr. LeSueur of the Post Office Department, who died a year or so ago, and who was a member of the Royal Society of Canada.

I cannot say as to that, I would be very glad to give my hon. friend the information if I had it.
The procedure adopted in connection with the War Lecture Bureau is to distribute a weekly bulletin containing information and material for speakers. This information goes to the clergymen of all denominations throughout Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It goes to public school inspectors, to school teachers, and to all volunteer speakers in connection with the War Lecture Bureau's work. I understand

that one hundred and fifty localities have been organized throughout Canada with speakers who undertake to give short talks, on the themes suggested for them, in moving picture shows,- theatres, Canadian clubs, and societies of all sorts; the object being to reach the people in this way with the living voice through pulpit, school, theatre and club.

May I ask, is this work along the same lines as that of the committee of one hundred sanctimonious gentlemen organized in Ontario as a general committee, With branches in every county in the province? Is this work along the same lines, and is if to be utilized for political purposes?

No, my hon. friend is quite in error. This bureau has nothing whatever to do with the committee to which he refers. Its work is just as I have explained. Perhaps I could not better define the work than by reading what President Falconer, of Toronto University, who is chairman of the advisory committee, has said. In a communication which I received from him in reference to the work, he states:	-
Since the beginning of December leaflets have been issued at frequent and fairly regular intervals dealing with themes which we thought would stimulate the mind of the people and give them useful information in regard1 to the war. These leaflets have gone to all the clergy of Canada, and to a large number of teaohers.
I have already stated that in some 150 localities (between the Atlantic and the Pacific, these local committees have been organized in the object of securing volunteer speakers who attend at the places which I have mentioned where they have the opportunity of addressing what they describe as really great audiences.
Sir SAM HLTGiHES: Can they get audiences to turn out to hear this sort of stuff?	.

They do apparently,
surprised as the hon. gentleman may he, and apparently the audiences enjoy it; I have a great many letters to that effect. However, this is what president Falconer says:
The experience of these months has demonstrated that there is a wide field of usefulness for such work. We know that both the army at -the front and the Government at home depend to a great extent upon the moral quality of the country. That quality is undoubtedly good, but under the severe strain which we are suffering at present endurance may flag unless it is stimulated. Courage and patience are needed in these critical months. The people must be informed and stimulated by

telling them facts that will strengthen their resolution by keeping before them regularly the purposes of the war, by cheering them as to tlie" accounts of its progress, or in times of darkness by buoying them up with hope, and by setting before them the plans of the Government which will contribute to the winning of the war. The hearts of the people must be kept high. Of course the debt that is owed to the newspapers is enormous, but there is need also of the spoken utterance, of the direct appeal to the people supported and authorized by the Government. We know what President Wilson has done in the Unitedi States and that Britain has appointed a Director of Propaganda. To this there are two sides, the press and organized public address.
President Falconer, and other men of like outstanding 'position in Canada, are freely giving voluntarily of their time and' their ability to carry on this propaganda at home in order that the spirit of the -Canadian people may be sustained clear and strong through these days of stress and struggle.
In order that my hon. friend may have some idea of the weekly bulletins which are sent out, let one draw attention to the last number issued' in which the subject is headed, " A Lesson from the Napoleonic Wars." If any hon. gentleman wish to read this 'bulletin I shall be glad to have them furnished with copies. 1 venture to think they will not find anywhere a better summary of the critical situation which existed during the 'Napoleonic wars, and of the position which 'Great Britain had to face at that time, vastly more serious than that which she faces to-day*. A message of courage an'di cheer such as this bulletin contains must necessarily be very helpful at the present time, and will reach thousands of people throughout -Canada in a direct and effective way through the volunteer speakers of the War Lecture Bureau.
This particular article was prepared by one of the best kno.wn professors of history in Canada who is glad to give his time and ability to this work.
The work of this department commands the confidence and support of patriotic citizens all over the country, who are deeply interested in the success of Canada in the war and* in sustaining the spirit of the Canadian -people. My hon. friend wishes to know how it is appreciated by the clergy. All over Canada, the clergy of all denominations have expressed appreciation of these statements sent to them, giving them information in connection with the war and subjects bearing directly upon the war. I have here page after page of letters which have been received from clergymen all over Canada, expressing "their appreciation of these bulletins-. Among the thousands of letters. I have one from Rev. Charles E.

Coughlin, of Assumption College, Sandwich, Ontario, who wrote to the Bureau the following letter:
May I ,-State that I am firmly convinced of [the [necessity of prosecuting the war with undiminished vigour. This conviction is based not only on patriotic premises but also on the religious principles which I as a Catholic Priest approve. Whenever I have an opportunity to address my fellow citizens or-co-religionists, be assured that I shall endeavour to inspire them with the "Win-the-War" spirit.
We also have letters from men like Principal Dyde, of Robertson College, Edmonton, who says:
You address willing ears. X am willing to do all in my power in pulpit and platform and will place myself at the disposal of any committee or council which is, or may be formed. This is without reserve.
If my hon. friends are interested, I have pages of extracts from letters from the foremost clergymen of all denominations from the Atlantic to the Pacific, thanking the bureau for sending them these weekly publications which they say contain valuable information. Man after man says that it should have been established before, that it helps them in presenting the facts to their congregations, Many clergymen living in out-of-the-way sections of the country, away from metropolitan centres, where the large papers do not circulate so freely, say that the information contained in these statements is of great value and that they use it Sunday after Sunday in presenting to their congregations the war situation and the demand upon our energies and resources which each day makes more urgent. I will not trouble the House with reading these communications unless my hon. friends wish [DOT] to have some of their contents presented to them.
Are those publications translated into French and circulated also in the province of Quebec?
They are.
By whom, may I ask?
Mr. Chairman-
I promised to -see the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburto-n next.

I was on my feet
when the hon. member who has just taken his seat concluded,, to dispose of another issue; and as I may not have the -privilege of being present to-night until late, I will take the occasion now. I want to say a few words regarding the position in which Colonel Armand Lavergne stands before the people of Canada. I hold no brief for Armand Lavergne. But I have had 'Arm-and Lavergne's speeches reported when- other gentlemen did not; I have had him interviewed when other gentlemen have not. Armand Lavergne's speeches and actions have been accepted by the party to which I had the honour to belong in the election of 1911.
Hear, hear.

And through the
exertion-s of Arm-and Lavergne and others of his ilk the Liberal Conservative party came into power, for the welfare of the country. I shall not enter into- further details now. Armand Lavergne is- an impulsive young fellow, the same as my good friend from Frontenao (Mr. Edwards), and as your humble servant, On- occasions, possibly, a little balance would do any one of us no harm. I have- had reported Armand Lavergne's speech that I understand was made in Quebec on. a certain occasion, with
[DOT]896

the o-bject of taking it up with the department if I could possibly find that he was using language that could foe construed by any lawyer into being treasonable. I have not failed-and as to this the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice will bear me out-to urge that, if there was any possibility of reaching him under the law, it should be done. So far as I am concerned, I have never yet found an occasion when he has uttered one treasonable word or one word that could foe construed as any worse than lots of language that has been published in the Toronto Globe and other standard publications of that kind. I am devoid of prejudice in this matter. Because Armand Lavergne is a Frenchman is no reason why he should, not have full justice. I have seen any number of these young French lads go over to the front and do splendid work there. And the trouble is not, as I view it-and I can speak ing frankly and fairly-because the French Canadian people are opposed to this war, but it is' chiefly because of the influence of the ultramontane wing of the Roman church in the province of Quebec-not the old, broad, tolerant, Bleu or the progressive, steadfast Liberal, or the radical wing- that the idea has been disseminated, largely through the influence of Bourassa t-o whom every one bows, which have held up enlistments on the present occasion. I think that is^the po-sition. I have no corner to turn on the subject. And if my hon. friend from Frontenac has the evidence that he claims he has, his duty is cleaT, and complaint should- foe lodged against Armand Lavergne, and he should foe arrested under the law and brought up for treason. So far as any personal references of the hon. gentleman to my asociation with Colonel J. Wesley Allison are concerned, I may say that history is already turning, the lane is being turned, and to-day J. Wesley Allison stands higher in the opinion of the British Government than do any of his detractors. He is consulted to-day by the British Government; he is of more assistance to-day to the British Government than all the gentlemen who have maligned him in this country or in the Empire.
He is of more importance in the eyes of the British officers to-day than are these gentlemen, or than any of them ever will be. The wheel of fortune, therefore, is taking a turn. I should not be surprised to see J. Wesley Allison a baronet if he keeps on.
As to the statement of my good friend the President of the Council, I will take the liberty of replying to it. In the first place,
TSir Sam Hughe*. 1
I understand that the gentleman whom he has chosen for Director of Public Information is a half-brother to the Minister of Finance, and is the same gentleman who edited the Montreal Daily Mail and the Montreal Evening News, two papers which were started with the definite object of booming the Finance Minister to be Prime Minister of Canada, getting rid of a gentleman who, they claimed, had no backbone, and incidentally maligning your humble servant on any and every occasion. I could imagine from the line on which he conducted the paper that the gentleman in question could not expect to commend himself to a great many of the people of this country who held other views than those to which he gave utterance. I object to the principle with which my hon. friend has associated himself. I do not especially know the gentleman concerned, so I will not deal with that aspect of the matter. The thing is in harmony, however, with an organization which has been engineered, I understand, largely by the hon. gentleman himself-a very good organization, but it does not work-to go into the counties. For instance, I understand that the organization was to have a committee of a certain number of men-one hundred, I think-to work for a little time when people do not get their eyes open. People are connected in the city of Toronto with those in various other parts of the province, and when the button is touched, politics and all else swing into the line laid down by my good hon. friend. It was tried in my county, but it did not work. The people of that county were too well posted; we had preceded our friends with literature of another [DOT] kind. All this solicitude may be good for the poor, innocent, ignorant people of the Dominion of Canada, but I have this faith and experience, that the good people living in the remote parts of the country are just as well posted on the causes of this war and how to carry it on as is the hon. gentleman who presides at the head of the Council, or many others of us who * may think that we know it all and that these people do not know anything. There was one of those gentlemen who cape into my riding. We took him out to the back part of the county to practise a little, and get his hand in, and he came back utterly amazed to think that 'the farmers could teach him many lessons in politics. The same thing may foe found all throughout Canada. This attempted solicitude, this paternalism, this hypnotism, this chloroforming that is going on throughout Canada among the great masses of the people is.

to my mind, absolute nonsense. The people are fully alive to the 'situation-those who could be impressed by this sort of thing,- and those who are not impressed must be reached by the legislation which we are bringing up to-morrow, bringing them out by compulsion. I have listened, of course, with great pleasure, to the complimentary remarks made by clergymen. I can easily realize how clergymen in the country districts would gladly get this stuff and unload it on their congregations on Sunday. It would save them the trouble of preparing a sermon, and would therefore be a very handy thing to have. However, so far as the practical use of it is concerned, it does not run in my line of practicability.

I have listened with a great deal of attention to the answer given to-day by the President of the Council to the objections which I urged the other evening against the appointment of Mr. Nichols. Much as we are indebted to the President of the Council for the elaborate explanation he has given, I still submit that a better choice could have been made; indeed, that the post was not needed at all. It is, shall I say a libel?-it is a libel on the press of this country to say that people in the faraway districts are not well informed, and that there must be a central bureau in Ottawa to impart to them information about the war. Mr. Chairman, I am a reader of the press; I was a member of the press in my younger days. 1 read the press of the United States. I read some of the papers published in England and in France, and that of the various provinces of Canada. I daresay that there are no better informed papers than those published in the large centres of Canada, and in the rural districts as well. On the question of the war, surely you can open any paper published in the rural sections of Canada and get just as much information as you will get in the daily press.	From	that point of view,
therefore, I do not think the appointment was needed. As regards the personality of Mr. Nichols, I have this to say: Mr. Nichols never impressed me as a successful man in his own business. It is a well-known fact that he killed two newspapers in Montreal because he could not gather the support of the Conservative party in Montreal by reason of his attempting to destroy my hon. friend the then 'Minister ot Militia (Sir Sam Hughes). He was also,
I must tell my hon. friend, mixed up in a very questionable business, when with his business partner he attempted to exnro-57	'	'
priate for this Government that hotel in Montreal known as the Carslake hotel. He asked the Government something like $600,000 or $700,000 for this building, which really was not needed by the Government, because the Post Office Department had a lot at a stone's throw from the Carslake hotel-a lot which was vacant, and had been purchased when Sir William Mulock was Postmaster General. Nevertheless, by his intrigues, he succeeded in landing that Carslake hotel on the Public Works Department. He was ready to get something like $700,000 from the Government, but when the expropriation proceedings took place in Montreal it was found that the whole building and the whole lot were not worth more than $150,000 or $200,000. I read the other day the sheet which my hon. friend held in his hands a moment ago. What is said tuere about Napoleon and Wellington and the battle of Waterloo as compared with the present struggle-why, it has been published time and again since the beginning of the war. The Prime Minister two years ago, in his speech delivered in this House, used exactly the'same parallel. You can find it in any third-class school history. In any back concession third-class school you will find that history of Waterloo and Wellington and Blucher and all the details about how many men were gathered there, and so on. Surely my hon. friend will not try to convince me that this is a chef d'oeuvre. I believe that to incur this expenditure is a pure waste of money, when the people of this country are straining every nerve to pay their tax bills, their income tax, and their customs dues. It is quite right to vote the money needed fox the carrying on of the war, but when it comes to creating fat offices for men who have been failures in their business, that is another matter. I am told by the ex-Minister of Militia that not only is this organization for giving information to the public on the question of the war, but that it is really nothing else but politics.

Might I correct the hon. member? I did not say that. I asked if it was in harmony with a kindred organization formed in the province of Ontario some years ago whereby my hon. friend would get in touch with the better elements of the country along certain lines, and then when he wanted to use them politically all he had to do was to push the button and the thing would go. I want to know the names of the men on the committee formed by the hon. gentleman.	[DOT]



iMbr. iLEiMIBTJX: The hon. minister can explain that himself. One aspect of the question which does not please me at all is that of the publication of the Record. In view of the huge amounts we shall, during this week, be called upon to vote, how can you expect, Sir-and I appeal especially to the Prime Minister-to have national unity in this country, when you ask the taxpayers of Canada, Liberals and Conservatives, to vote money for publications in which one-half of the people of Canada are being libelled and slandered? After the last election I received from my son, who was at Witley Camp, a bundle of those Records containing the vilest statements about my right hon. leader and about the French Canadian generally. Do you believe, Sir, that the publication of that Record is a national necessity? The elections are over. The Record did its work in the trenches in the last campaign. Drop it, for Heaven's sake; we do not want it any more. If you want to have the respect, the backing, of the country for the huge sums, which you are asking us to vote and for the stringent measures which you are taking in order to make the Military Service Act more effective, for decency's sake do not ask the people who are being slandered and libelled to say " amen " to such nonsense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should like very much to. see the issues of the Record to which my hon. friend refers, and which, according to his conception, contained vile slanders upon the Tight hon. leader of the Opposition and upon French Canadians. They have never been brought to my attention. So far as this newspaper is concerned, I am not aware that any public money of Canada is paid out for its publication, except that which is expended in sending messages containing news from Canada for the men at the front. When the hon. gentleman talks about abolishing the Record, I should like to tell him that according to my information every man in the Canadian forces at the front would protest against the idea of abolishing the Record, because it is the chief means they have of getting home news from day to day. I think those who have served at the front will beaT me out in that.
In regard to a question which was asked, I think, by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), with respect to a list which appeared in the Daily Record of the candidates at the last election, I may 
isay that that subject was brought to my attention some time ago by the War Veterans' Association, I think, and I made inquiry concerning it. The inquiry was made by the director of public information at my request. I sent for him and asked him to investigate. He has given me this memorandum in reply, and it is proper that the House .should know it. This is a memorandum from Captain William Wallace, M.C., Officer in Charge for Canada, Canadian Daily Record, regarding publication of nomination list in the Canadian Daily Record:
On November 14, 1917, I received a cable from the Canadian War Records Office, London, asking me to see that a complete list of nomi-ations throughout Canada was sent overseas and to indicate the time it would1 be available so they could (prepare for an enlarged issue.
I replied stating the Government was required by law to send a list of nominations overseas and that I was informed that the General Returning Officer would cable the list to Colonel Pumey, c/o High Commissioner's Office, about November 20.
I suggested the list oould' be obtained from Ool. Purney, my idea being to save cable tolls from this office. On November 15th I received a cable saying this arrangement would be satisfactory and that the Canadian War Records Office would arrange to get the list from Col. Purney.
Therefore, no official list of nominations was sent from this office.
When the question of the omission of certain names from the nomination list published in the Canadian Daily Record was brought up by the newspapers here, I cabled the Canadian War Records Office on February 27, 1918, asking if any explanation could be given why the names of McCormack, (Parkdale) ; Cock-burn, (East York) ; (McLaren, (West Hamilton) ; and Sutherland, (North Oxford), were not included in the nomination list published in the Canadian Daily Record on November 27th.
Was the name of Mr. Harry Cookshutt, of Brant, in the list?

speechtext: I am reading the memorandum. If my hon. friend will be good enough to withhold any questions until *I get through with the memorandum I shall be pleased' to answer them.
The Prime Minister is reading the names.

speechtext:

Dear Captain Wallace:

We received the list that was published on November 27th from Colonel Purney who was in charge of the election here, and I understand that he received it direct from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Two days later he sent us a revised list and we issued a special revised Nomination Edition of the Canadian Daily Record, which was dated Thursday, November 29th, and which contained all the names you mention.
The distribution was the same in each case, so that everyone who read the first list also [DOT] had the opportunity to read the revised list.
I send you herewith a dozen copies of the November 29th issue in case you would like to send them to the newspapers who have taken up the matter with you.

At six o'clock
I was giving some explanation in regard to the issues of the Canada War Record of 27th and 29th November. I have nothing to add in regard to that. But, there are one or two words which I would like to say in regard to the Director of Public Information. The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has found some fault with

his appointment for the Teason that he alleges he wae connected in some way with the purchase of a property in Montreal, the value of -which was not fixed by the Government but was fixed by the Exchequer Court. II am perfectly confident-II have Mr. Nichols' word for it-that he had no more interest in that property than had the hon. member for Maisonneuve and that he had no more to do with fixing the value than had that hon. gentleman.
Some comment was also made on the fact that he is a relative of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). I happened to know something of the way in which Mr. Nichols was appointed. My hon. friend the president of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) brought to my attention, and to the attention of his colleagues, the proposal for the establishment of a directorship of public information. He has set out the reasons this afternoon on account of Which he thought that proposal would be a valuable one in the public interest. He mentioned to me the name of Mr. Nichole and I am in a position to state that the Minister of Finance had no more to do with the appointment of Mr. Nichols than any hon. gentleman in this. House. Mr. 'Nichols was not appointed in any way on account of his relationship, nor did the Minister of Finance know anything at all about it until the matter was proposed in Council by the President of the Privy Council. I think it is only right and just to Mr. Nichols, and to the Minister of Finance as well, to make that public statement in this House.
Further, as to the editorial policy of newspapers in Montreal with -which Mr. Nichols is said to have been connected, I am not in a position to epeak or to give any opinion upon that policy. Ae a matter of fact, I do not have time to read newspapers at all except an occasional bunch of clippings that is handed to me by one of my secretaries. But I do positively assert that I am as confident as I am of my own existence that the Minister of Finance had no more to do with the editorial policy of any of these papers in Montreal than any hon. gentleman who is listening to me in this House.

While the Prime Minister is discussing this question, would he have any objection to telling the House and the country who were consulted previous to the appointment of Mr. Nichols? Last week, during the debate, the President of the Privy council (Mr. Rowell), stated that before appointing Mr. Nichols he had consulted

the best newspaper men in Canada, and that upon their recommendation he had appointed Mr. Nichols because that gentleman was known as a competent newspaper man. I understand that a great many of the best newspaper men in Canada say they were not consulted. Who were the newspaper men who were consulted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Inasmuch as I was not the person consulting them, I am afraid that I cannot give my hon. friend the information. We were assured by the President of the Privy Council that he had made the necessary inquiry and he was 30 advised.

This Bill is to provide for a military expenditure of $500,000,000. I would like to know what portion of the total amount is to cover the expenses in excess of the war appropriation of 1917 and also the amount that is required for the military operations of this year. 'I understand that with the amount required for this year the Government is taking into consideration additional expenditures to be incurred by the amendments contemplated to the Military Service Act, 1917, which appear in the Government's notice of motion on the Orders of the Day the debate upon which has been adjourned until to-morrow. I maintain that this is not the proper time to discuss in Committee of the House the Bill providing for the appropriation of that large amount. We see by these proposed resolutions that the Government intends to make some amendments to the Military Service Act. It follows that the expenses of the current year will be increased if these resolutions are adopted by Parliament. I hope they will not be adopted by Parliament, but if they are adopted there is no doubt that the appropriation for next year will have to be increased accordingly. I should say that inasmuch as the appropriation of $500,000,000 is for the putting into operation of conscription, I am against it. I have been elected against conscription and I am against all forms of conscription. I would expect that the Government would defer the consideration of this Bill until the proposed amendments to the Military Service Act. now before the House, are taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will look at the statement that I read in the House, page 597 of unrevised Hansard, he will see that the accounts up to the present time, as far as they can be furnished to us by the Finance Department, show a total of $306,488,814.63 from which it would appear that no portion of this sum will be needed to meet the expenditure of the last fiscal year. 'If. however, the accounts when they come in should swell the total to more than $500,000,000 this Bill provides that any balance may be paid out of it.
Is it contemplated to provide out of the $500,000,000 for the additional cost of carrying out the military lew as it is supposed to be amended this session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman probably is aware that the Military Service Act provides for raising a total force of one hundred thousand men. The estimate that I have already given takes into account the one hundred thousand men to be raised under the Military Service Act.

Has the Government any idea as to how the account of Canada with Great Britain stands to-day? I understand that we are paying for certain things on behalf of the British Government which are being manufactured or produced in and shipped from this country. I understand we are paying in Canada for certain things that ought to be paid by Great Britain. We may not be actually advancing the money because there is a somewhat similar financial process being followed on the other side in our interest. Has any balance been struck between the British Government and the Dominion Government, and does the balance stand to the credit or the debit of the British Government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Early in the war the British Government made a loan, not a very large loan, to Canada. Upon the accounts as they stand at present I believe the balance is in favour of Canada, but I am not sure of the exact amount. What happens is this: the British Government pays accounts for us in connection with the maintenance of our troops at the front, provides supplies and so forth, which I suppose would run up to something like $200,000,000 a year, or very nearly that. On the other hand, we provide in this country credits for tihe British Government in payment for munitions, food stuffs, and supplies of various kinds, and those, of course, are charged against the British Government, just as the amounts that they advance are charged against us. Upon the whole, since the beginning of the war, the balance is something in favour of Canada.

I understood from a statement made the other day, that the British Government was paying for our troops in France at the rate of six shillings a day per man, and that that covered munitions, equipment and everything. Is the British Government paying for our troops in England and is there, as in the case of the troops in France, a stated per capita amount which the British Government is advancing on our account?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The arrangement to which I have alluded applies only to the tioops in France.
And the six shillings covers everything?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The six shillings
covers everything, but I again remind my hon. friend that the other Dominions of the Empire have agreed to increase that to something over nine shillings, I think. We have not yet given our formal consent, but it is very likely that in all fairness we shall be obliged to do so, because of the tremendous increase in the use of shells and munitions of all kinds which has come about since that arrangement was entered into. I would like also to remind the hon. gentleman that the accounts have not yet been adjusted. When I state my belief that the balance is in favour of Canada, I make that statement subject to the final adjustment of accounts.

I would like the Prime Minister to take his pencil and make a calculation, because I have some figures that require explanation. I see that the expenditure during the first year of the war, 1914-1915, on account of naval service was

$3,096,125. During the second year, 19151916, the expenditure in round figures was $3,274,000, and in the third year, 1916-1917, the expenditure was approximately $3,806,000, whereas last year, up to April the 8th, the expenditure on account of naval service reached a total of over $10,000,000 in round figures. There seems to be quite an increase there, and the committee is entitled to an explanation of why there is such a difference. I am simply speaking of the expenditure on the naval service, I shall have other questions to submit Jater as to the expenditure under other heads.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's question is a very reasonable one, and I will give an explanation of it as far as it is possible to do so in the public interest. In the autumn of 1916, I think it was, the Government of Canada was called upon very suddenly by the Admiralty to take certain precautions in connection with the theatened submarine menace against the coasts of this country. We consulted with them, and steps were taken with very great promptness, and in the most effective way possible, by the then Minister of Naval Affairs, Mr. Hazen. Those steps involved a very considerable outlay at once in the provision of trawlers, patrol boats and other armed vessels, in order that the merchant marine of Canada might be protected so far as possible from any attack by submarines near our coasts. I do not know that I can go into the matter more fully at the moment, but I am confident that the minister in charge of the Naval Service will be very glad indeed to give the hon. gentleman privately much fuller information than it would be prudent to publicly disclose in this House. The expenditures of last year are grouped in an account which I shall he glad to send over to the hon. gentleman if he cares to look at it. It is not desirable, I think, that l should do more or give some information the publication of which is undesirable, Altogether, these expenditures amount to $10,662,981.02.

lyTIr. LEMIEUX: I find that the Military ' Hospitals Commission in 1916-17 cost $1,378,000, in round figures, while last year the cost was over $9,000,000. What is the explanation of the increase?

The Minister of Militia and Defence will be in a position to give full information on that subject.

Are there many employees?

This Order in Council was the one which prohibited men of military age from leaving the country. A further amount of $8,000 is mentioned under the head of printing and stationery- that is, for printing the different permit forms and any stationery required by the officers.
There is an item of $399,266.89 under the heading: " Railways and Canals, reconstruction of Halifax." Was that for the emergency call when the Halifax disaster took .place?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
