There has been presented during the war the greatest opportunity the department ever had, in conjunction with the Department of Agriculture, to encourage the horse industry in this country. If I am correctly informed, the department has not taken advantage of this opportunity. I believe that horses are being purchased for Great Britain in the United States, and have been going through Canada in thousands. I wish to call attention to the fact that m 1916-17 there was spent by the Militia Department on war account, according to the public accounts, the very large sum of $298,000,000. I put a question on the Order Paper as to what amount of money had been .spent in the purchase of remounts for the Militia Department during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1917, and the answer was $261,042.73. I further inquired what amount was spent in the purchase of remounts elsewhere, and where they were purchased, to which the reply was " nil." In the public accounts for 1917, under

the heading of " Details of War Expenditure by Militia Department" from April 1, 1916, to March 31, 1917, I find an item:	Purchases of remounts, expenses of purchasers, etc., $3,440,761.64. I should like some explanation of that discrepancy and also some statement of policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have already given that explanation a good many times, not only in this Parliament, but in the late Parliament. I gave it two years ago for the first time, and 1 have given it on several occasions since. When I was in England in 1915 it was arranged that all remount purchases for the Canadian Expeditionary Force should be made- iby the British Government. They had a very competent staff engaged both in Canada and in the United States for that purpose. Further than that, unless we arranged the matter in that way, we would be obliged to keep up remount stations at various points in Great Britain and also at various points in France; whereas, if the Temount stations, from which we would get our horses, both in Great Britain and France were under one control, a very great expense would1 be saved to this country. The British Government agreed that they would put in the horses to us at bare cost. In fact, in their charges against the horses which they supplied to us- they did not include what might he called overhead charges, which would necesarily have been included by this country if we had embarked upon a policy of having separate remount stations of our own both in Great Britain and France. Therefore, the expenditure to which my hon. friend calls attention is expenditure which has been made by the British Government for horses purchased in that way by a commission acting for both parties. The other item to which he alluded, namely, $261,042.73 is for horses used in the various camps in Canada and not for horses used overseas. I am informed by the deputy minister that 2,876 horses were purchased for the purpose of those camps.
With respect to- the opportunities in Canada for the sale of horses; I have had very frequent correspondence with the British Remount Commission. From- time to time since 1915 I have not failed to urge upon them directly and also through the British Government that there were good opportunities for the purchase of horses in this country, and that those opportunities should be taken advantage of by the British Remount Commission, and on every occasion on which I have taken uR the matter with

the Remount Commission they have given what semed to me to be a satisfactory explanation when they did not happen to be purchasing in Canada at that time.

I was asking, when the other questions were put, what arrangement existed1 as to the balancing of accounts between Great Britain and Canada. I see that the overseas forces which are now in England are paid for by Canada. The Prime Minister, the other day in making an explanation, said that the expenditure overseas was under the supervision of the Auditor General. Has the Auditor General a staff overseas auditing those accounts *which are paid by the Overseas Minister of Militia? If so, when is a return made to the Minister of Militia .at Ottawa so that he may control the expenditure which is voted for war purposes or for supplying the troops which we have in England-that is, in addition to the balance which we have to strike with Great Britain with reference to the troops, that we have in France? The current accounts of the Minister of Overseas Military Forces, I understand, are controlled by the Auditor General. The ultimate control comes to Ottawa, and I suppose that the Minister of Militia, .as I said the other day when i was expressing my astonishment at this duplication, is responsible to the House for that. Can we have an explanation of the system that is followed?-how these amounts are controlled overseas, how the return of this expenditure is made, and to whom it is made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Just the same as in any other department. The accounts are audited overseas by the Auditor General. I do not think he has any staff in Great Britain at the present time; that is, for the Teason that he does think it necessary. When I stpoke to him a few days ago, he said that his officer had returned from England; that his officer was not there during the winter, and he did not consider it necessary to keep him there. That is a matter which we leave to his own judgment. He had an absolutely free hand to have whatever staff was necessary, according to his best judgment, to make a thorough and complete audit of all the expenditures overseas. The statements come forward from that department just the same as from other departments, and I believe, besides that, a monthly statement comes to the Department of Militia and Defence as well as to the Auditor General.

I do not say this in the way of criticism, except that I cannot get
through my head this double Ministry of Militia, particularly in regard to the Overseas Minister. What is the approximate amount that has been handled and expended by the Minister of Overseas Military Forces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The expenditure overseas from 4th August, 1914, to 31st of March, 1917, amounted to $171,137,853.86. That, of course, did not include the expenditure in France to which I have already alluded and which is made by the British Government on behalf of the Canadian Government.
iMr. FIELDING:	Perhaps the information about which I am going to inquire has already been given, and if it is in Hansard,
I do not wish to have the right hon. gentleman repeat it. I presume this appropriation, which is necessarily a very broad one, included expenditures in connection with the mission at Washington?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It would be included in this appropriation.

The mission at Washington is one of the many new things which have been created during the war, and the public would like to have some information concerning it. I would, therefore, suggest that, at a convenient date, not necessarily at the present time, the right hon. gentleman might give us some information as to the number of persons composing the mission, their salaries and the nature of the duties they are called upon to perform. .Some part of their duties may have a bearing upon military matters and, of course, the information in regard to that cannot be given. I put my question with' that reservation. I am sure the subject would be an interesting one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon friend perhaps did not observe that some time ago I placed upon the Table an Order in Council which gives the principal part of the information to which he alludes. Mr. Lloyd Harris, is the Chairman. There are at the present time only three other gentlemen upon the board, namely, Mr. Rolph, of Toronto, Mr. Macmaster, and Mr. Scott, of Montreal. They are all serving without any salary whatever, though of course they have a clerical staff, and there will be some expense incurred for renlt, which unfortunately is very high in Washington at present. The duties are defined in a general way in the Order in Council, a copy of which I shall be very glad to

send to my hon. friend. II shall be very glad after that, to go a little more into detail, as to the particular purposes which this War Mission is carrying out. They have very important duties to 'perform,. Those duties are more directly concerned with communication between the very numerous commissions which have been established, in Washington, and Iwhich have to do in a very intimate way with the trade relations between this country and the United States as they are affected by the war, the import and export of articles, the restriction of importations to articles of an essential character, the utilization of industries of both countries for purposes that are essential for the war and not for other purposes, and a great many other matters which I shall be glad to explain at some later date.
