If the Prime Minister is not aware of .it, I can tell him that [DOT]there were other names in the list that were initialled neither by the leader of the Opposition nor by himself, and these names appeared in the first list.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was not aware of that.

But it .is correct, because I know that the name of the candidate in .my Tiding who was running against me was on the list. There were three candidates drl that riding, and the names of both my opponents appeared in this first official Hist, as well as my own. This is war time, land I am not disposed to raise any trouble, or give this Government any trouble that can be avoided, but the element of fairness cannot be overlooked even in a war-time election; and I must say that the Prime Minister's explanation so far as those names are concerned, is not satisfactory to me. Other names went over that were not so initialled. I can give the name of one, and I believe there were five or sax others. To say that the list was reprinted and sent over two days later does not cover the ground at all. This document, which I understand the President of the Privy Council is responsible for, is the official mouthpiece of the Government for the soldiers at the front. It was sent out containing certain names. We are told it was sent out in the first place on 27th November, and that after the mistakes were pointed out, it was reprinted and another copy sent on 29/th November; but we do not know when that copy .sent out on the 29th reached the front, or whether it ever reached the front. What we do know is that the soldiers began to vote on or about 1st December, although the election was not until the 17th, and I believe in imy heart that there were a lot of soldiers who never knew what candidates were running in that election. I feel that that was the case, and I say it was not necessary for the purposes of Union Government, of which I am a strong friend and backer, even though I make this criticism, that the names of .their candidates should be known. The soldier ballot had four divisions .in it-one for the Government candidate, one for the opposition candidate, one for labour, and one for an independent candidate.

I think there were five
divisions.

In the fifth space the name of the candidate was to be written,

or else he got no vote at all. So the soldier voted tor o*r against the Government, but where a candidate's niame was suppressed the soldier,, of course, had no opportunity of knowing that this man was running at all. I do not tike to accuse 'the powers that be of doing anything unfair or unjust, and in war time when we are fighting with our back to the- wall and our boys are dying by the thousands at the front it is no time to raise trouble. I want to back the Government for all I am worth in all war-time measures, but I do say that I think they were derelict in their duty. I did not even hear the Prime Minister say this afternoon that he had given the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery a crack over the knuckles for omitting the names of these candidates-names which I believe were deliberately omitted by some one. If that is the case it is a serious thing. It is all right for the Government and the Opposition to endorse their candidates, but in a democratic country, where a man is properly nominated and is of sufficient standing in the community to get the nomination, I think no Government and no Opposition has the right to suppress that man's name as a candidate for a seat in the House of Commons. I do not want to go into this matter very fully, and I do not want any of my friends to take any particular notice of it, because a member of my family was one of those concerned, but I do say that this kind of thing would only pass in the strenuous times through which we.are passing; that is the only ground on which we can keep quiet about a thing like that. It is the strenuous times in which we live that closes my mouth tonight, but I think it is up to me to let the Prime Minister know-yes, and the President of the Privy Council too, because I believe he was privy to the matter-that I thought at that time before this action was taken that it was going to turn out just about the way it has, that certain men were marked for slaughter, and that is how it did turn out. Whether this was a deal between the gentlemen I am not in a position to isay, because I am not in the inner circle, I am only a back-bencher. But I feel it my duty to say to the Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council that if it were not that winning the war demands our every exertion, I could not support them on this occasion. The Prime Minister may have other reasons up his sleeve which he did not adduce why these names were omitted. He may tell me as soon as I sit down that I am talking
entirely aside from the facts, but I thought it my duty to say that in my judgment his explanation given in regard to the lists of candidates sent overseas was entirely inadequate to the situation, and will not be at all satisfactory to the gentlemen whose names were suppressed from the official lists.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I shall not follow my hon. friend's advice, however much inclined I might be to do so. I shall merely tell him that I was not in Ottawa at the time. If he supposed that during that election I had nothing else to do but follow around the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and see that all his telegrams were correct, then. I can only say he has a very imperfect appreciation of the burdens that were laid on one at the head of public affairs in this country, when he was called upon at the same time to carry on as best he could the. (work in connection with the greatest war that humanity lias ever known and also to carry on an election campaign. If the hon. gentleman intends to suggest- and I do not know whether or not he did intend to suggest-that I was privy to any unfairness towards him, or any member of his family, or any one else, I want to give him the strongest denial that parliamentary usage will permit.

Did the right hon.
gentleman write a letter asking a certain gentleman to run and afterwards turn him down?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yee, I did in
this sense, that I suggested to him, at the request of an hon. gentleman, a member of the Senate, just .about the time the Union Government was formed, that he might run. That gentleman wrote to me afterwards and said that he would retire if I aeked him. I asked him to retire and he did not do. it.

That gentleman
offered to retire in favour of a certain other gentleman, as the Prime Minister very well knows, but not in favour of the one who was crushing him out of the field where he had been properly placed. The Prime Minister, if he wanted that letter read here, would find it very necessary to give me the direct statement that he has given just now. The letter was fairly and squarely written and it contained that statement. Whether the Prime Minister did it unknowingly or whether he did it with the intention, of asking him finally to retire., I cannot say, but it seems to me that we have not been

played fair with. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) has just raised .another question which involves more or less the same matter. One gentleman who was concerned in this matter has been rewarded with the chairmanship of a commission at Washington. How that comes about I cannot say, but that has been revealed to- us.
I have been a friend of the right hon. gentleman all my political life; during all his political life I have supported him. in every way; I have supported in every possible. way the winning of the war, and I take no back seat, although I am a back bencher, even to the Prime Minister him-seslf in regard to the heartiness in which I have endeavoured to help win this war. The Prime Minister, knowing what my family has, done in this matter, should cast no reflection on me in that respect, as I rather think he did. He seemed to say: You think I have nothing to do- but help to win elections. _ I made no such assertion. I say that in my judgment those names were suppressed by somebody-I do not know by whom-and the clerk of the Crown in Chancery, if he were in any way responsible, should have received a crack Over the knuckles for sending out an imperfect list.
I have not heard the Prime Minister say one word of disapproval, or whether he disapproves of an imperfect list being sent out. He has not the right to read me a lecture, even although I am a back-bencher; I am a pretty old hand in the political game. I was in it before he was. I ran my first campaign over thirty years ago. Although I do not often speak in this House, and although my views may not carry very much weight, even with the Prime Minister-I am aware of that-I still have my views and they are held, just as strongly as are those of the Prime Minister. In so far as the winning of the war is concerned, 1 believe that my heart is in it just as much as his is. Our object is to win the war and that was the object with which we went into the war-time election, but even a war-time election should, in my judgment, be characterized by all the elements of fairness.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was just that suggestion on the part of the hon. gentleman that I did resent because he seemed to imply that there had been some intentional unfairness on my part through which these gentlemen's names were not included in the first telegram. I repeat that I resent as strongly as I can any unfair sug-
gestion from him or any one else in this House. I have told him-he is at liberty to take my statement or not as he sees fit- that I was not in Ottawa at the time and knew nothing until months afterward about any names being omitted from the list. I repeat that I was far too busily engaged at that time to follow up the details of any such matter as this. The task of selecting candidates in the various constituencies of this country who should be recognized by the Government was an invidious and distasteful one. Few hon. gentlemen can realize how invidious and distasteful it would be. I did the best I could with it. I appointed a committee in each of the provinces composed of men who previously had been opposed to each other in political affairs, and I asked them to make the best selections they could. As far as I remember, I foljowed their judgment in every case; I do not recollect any case in which I departed from it. Whether I might have done better by giving more personal attention to the matter I do not know. I do know that I did what I thought was right and what I thought was- best in the interest of the country and without any desire or intention of being unfair to any man, whether he was recognized or not.

As the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has mentioned my name in connection with this matter, as well as that of the Prime Minister, I wish to state just as clearly and emphatically as the Prime Minister has stated that I had absolutely no knowledge of the matter until weeks after the election. The first I learned of it was from a statement which I saw in the press some time after the election that these names had been omitted from the list. I, like the Prime Minister, had been absent from Ottawa, and I never had any communication of any kind with the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. He is not in my department and I had no communication with him. On learning of this report after the election I asked for an explanation from the general returning officer and I got one similar to that which the Prime Minister has given the House this afternoon. I had no knowledge about it in any shape or form, direct or indirect, until long after the election.
Does the minister approve or disapprove of the action of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery in omitting those names?

I absolutely disapprove of any names being omitted. I am absolutely sure that they were omitted by mistake although I have no personal knowledge of it. Every one would disapprove of any names being omitted. Every one should have a fair show; the names should all be made public.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I omitted to say the same thing. I regard it as most unfortunate that the names were omitted and if it were owing to any intentional neglect on the part of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery he would be subject to the severest reprimand and probably something more than that.
Mr. MO WAT; I desire to say a few words to the committee in regard to the effect of this omission. I will confine myself to that. It appears that owing to the information telegraphed by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery certain names were omitted. That was corrected two days afterwards. The two issues o.f the Record were on the 27th and 29th November. If there was ahy objection to that action, or if there was any injustice, some complaint would have been made from France or England regarding it by the friends of the candidates whose names were omitted. But was that done? No, it was not. It was not until two months after 27th November that the matter was mentioned at all. And how did it come to be mentioned at all? It was mentioned by a newspaper in Toronto which had taken a very strong stand on behalf of what it called the "soldier candidates." The Prime Minister said this afternoon that he had received some complaints with regard to the matter from the Great War Veterans, but I desire to correct him to some extent in that regard. The Great War Veterans as a body, wisely it seems to me, decided to take no part in party politics; their interests, they thought, required that they should stand neutral; but an ambitious gentleman in Toronto who runs a newspaper had different views. He has always been very distinctly antagonistic and hostile to the Union Government. Holding such views and having no chance with the Opposition he could not satisfy his inordinate ambition to become a political leader unless he had some sort of a party. The only party he could think of to get was the Great War Veterans. Now the resolution of the Great War Veterans to take no part in politics stood as a bar to their becoming followers of any body, himself or any body else.
Therefore, the gentleman in question got an employee of his own newspaper, who [DOT] happens to be the secretary of a local branch of the Great War Veterans, to have the resolution of the main body sitting here in , Ottawa rescinded, so that the Toronto branch of the Great War Veterans' Association should be able to engage in party politics in this contest. The Great War Veterans area fine body of men as a whole. They are men who went to serve their country, and some of them have come back maimed or nervous as a result of shell shock. The trouble is that being nervous and somewhat sentimental they art apt to be misled, and in this ease they were misled, it seems to me, not by one of their own number, not by a soldier, but by a person who wished to use them for his own purposes. Perhaps I am a little discursive, but I wish to point opt that the effect of this mistake in not publishing these names in the first number of The Record cannot have had any real or practical effect. In the first place, as I say, no attention was called to it for months after 27th November, and furthermore, during the election the same band of civilians who wished to intrude and make a sort of a third party as part of their election campaign, said to the people:	"We have
sent over cables to the soldiers at the front." They did send many cables and in one election of which 1 have knowledge they said they spent something over $200 upon cable tolls. " Therefore," they said " don't be troubled by the fact of endorsation by the Union Government, but vote for our candidate and you will find that a vast number of soldiers at the front will join with you and he will be elected." Well, with the expenditure of $200 in the case of one candidate, one would have thought that the soldiers at the front would have been informed of the exact state of affairs. What do we find? According to the election returns, a copy of which we got a few days ago from Mr. O'Connor, in the particular constituency I refer to the endorsee of the Government got 3,300 overseas votes. How many do you suppose were cast for the soldier candidate, to whom not only the particular issue of The Record had reference, but in whose interest there had been an expenditure of $200 in sending cablegrams to soldiers at the front. As against 3,300 votes for the Unionist candidate, the soldier candidate only received 13 votes in the whole of France and in England, so the omission referred to cannot have had much to do with the result.
There is another constituency, represented by my hon. friend the member for

East York (Mr. Foster). That hon. gentleman was subjected to vicious attack. I make no complaint whatever of any attack made upon me in the election. If my opponents consider such attacks are fair politics, all right. I make no complaint, whatever, especially as I won by a jolly good* majority. But in the case of my hon. friend from East "York as vitriolic and acidulous an attack was made upon him as was ever known in Canadian politics, and he was deprecated in every form as a miserable civilian running against this nominee of the new party that I have referred to. Well, the result in bis case, where antagonistic cablegrams were also sent over to the front, was more extraordinary than in the ease of the other constituency I have mentioned; because, while my hon. friend received more than 2,700 votes in England and in France, the soldier candidate who ran against him, did not get one single vote. So it was a case of 2,700 votes to nothing. The point of my remarks is this,: despite the mistake made-I am sure it was a mistake, because nobody could be a party to actually misleading the electors over there-the actual fact is that the soldiers were not misinformed, they knew who was running, but they deliberately marked their ballots for the Government because they knew that would suit their purpose far better than any other course they could take.
[Mr. REDMAN: I cannot but regard it as unfortunate that the hon. member who has just taken his seat should have seized this Opportunity to ask for the sympathy of the House in regard to the election which he ran last year. I oannot but resent the statements which he has made in regard to the Great War Veterans, and, as I take it, the soldiers generally. It strikes me that his remarks were in very bad taste. The fact that a soldier ran against him in that election should not give him any Teason to come here and single out that soldier, or the Great War Veterans, for comments in this House. He has stated that the soldiers who have returned from overseas are sentimental and nervous. Doubtless the hon. gentleman is an authority on this subject, and when he states that the soldiers returning from overseas are sentimental and nervous, possibly the hon. gentleman knows what he is talking about, and possibly he does not. However, I do Tesent very much the hon. gentleman making any statements of the kind. It does seem to me that if the Great

War Veterans' Association, or any of their members wish to run a candidate in this country, or to exercise their rights as citizens, they are perfectly free to do so.
' Mr. SUTHERLAND: When this matter first came up a few hours ago the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) was making a statement with regard to the Director of Public Information. I asked him then as to who was responsible for the omission of the names of certain soldier candidate's in the last election from the, Canadian Daily Records sent to the soldiers, but I little thought at the time that my question was going to create the debate that has taken place. I regret very much, indeed, that the time of the House should be taken up with a matter that now can do no earthly good, because this is war time, and we have men at the front who are making greater sacrifices possibly than any one who have remained in Canada, no matter how hard such persons have laboured.
I intend, therefore, totouchupon one phase of the question that appeals to me, and that is on behalf of a certain soldier candidate in the last election; who was the first man to volunteer in the county of Oxford, who went overseas with the First Contingent, who raised two battalions in the country, was twice wounded, came home, and returned to the front crippled but determined to go. He was nominated as a candidate when he was at home on sick leave, and told the people that, if his election depended upon his returning to Canada while the war was on, he did not want to be elected. Now, for some strange reason, this candidate's name was omitted from the official list sent out by the Government in this official organ which we are asked to support in this vote which is now before the House; and, so far as I am aware, there is no disposition on the part of the Government to fix the responsibility where it properly belongs and to see that the guilty suffer for their misdeeds in this regard; at least, we had no expression of that kind from the Government to my knowledge. Men who are absent at the front fighting for us are not in a position to take up their cause in this House or in the country, or have not shown any disposition, or made any request, that the matter should be brought to the attention of the House, and, so far as I am aware, no complaint has been received from those men with regard to that matter. Now, the President of the Privy Council has just made a further statement that he knew

nothing whatever with regard to this matter, and I accept his word. He says that he was busily engaged at the time, and he does not know anything with regard, to the matter. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) brings the War Veterans into this debate, endeavouring to, make it appear that they renounced their rights during the last election. The War Veterans an Oxford county called an open convention to nominate a candidate, and I believe there were some six hundred people present to nominate a Unionist candidate. On the other side, his opponent was selected by the executive of the Liberal Party, and endorsed by the Government as the Unionist candidate in opposition to the man who had been nominated in an open convention called for that purpose. There is a feeling abroad in the country among returned soldiers that this Government is not in sympathy with the soldiers, that they are not doing certain things that they ought to do with regard to the returned soldiers. When you find things of this kind happening right under your eyes, I do not feel that it is my duty to sit still and allow statements of that kind to go unchallenged. Further, I believe that there was a deliberate effort on the part of some one to see that certain soldier candidates were not elected, and who ever is guilty-and there is certainly some guilty party-must be punished or else professions of being in sympathy with the soldier and with winning this war will stand for little. The men who are doing these things are entitled to consideration. When the campaign was nearing its close, certain correspondence was published with regard to one of these soldier candidates, in an endeavour to make it appear that he was not endorsed by the Government or as favouring Union Government. iBut his opponent, who had been selected by the executive of the Liberal party, was endorsed by the Government as the Unionist candidate. What do we find? On the 5th day of November, a letter from the secretary of the President of the Privy Council was published shedding more light on this matter, and making it practically impossible for that candidate to be elected in that constituency. I am going to read the letter; it has been published, and no denial has been made with reference to it to my knowledge. The Prime 'Minister has told us of his efforts, and of the work that was entailed upon him in endorsing candidates. I have not the slightest doubt of that. I appreciate the tremendous responsibilities that press upon the head of a Government, particularly during war time.
It is beyond my comprehension how he could do as much work as he did: consequently, he must have had to delegate a great deal of his work to others. I do not think for one moment he was responsible or that he would do anything of that nature. But I want to point out that the soldier candidate to whom I have referred did not receive a fair deal in the last election, and that a letter was sent to the secretary of the Conservative Association for the North Riding of Oxford, asking that the nominee of that party should be withdrawn. I understand that he was communicated with and offered to withdraw in order thct the Thggident of the Council (Mr. Rowell) might be elected for that constituency which he represented in the legislature. He offered to stand aside and allow that hon. gentleman to run in that riding. Later on,-he was nominated at this open convention. In the meantime, however, a letter was published in the press which had considerable effect upon his prospects of being elected. Now, I must read the letter, because I am going to read one that was sent out afterwards. This is written from Uxbridge on November 26, 1917:
Dear Mr. West,
I had hoped to apeak in North Oxford but the time at my disposal would not permit. Under the circumstances I think it my duty to ask my friends in the North Riding of Oxford to support loyally and effectively Mr. E. W. Nesbitt, the candidate named hy the Government under the Military Voters' Act. His support of compulsory military service and of the proposals for a Union Government has been all that could he desired. We are asking Liberals in a great many ridings of Ontario to support Conservative Union candidates. It is equally the duty of Conservatives to support Liberal Union candidates in the ridings for which, under arangement with my Liberal colleagues, a Liberal Union candidate has been, selected.
Believe me,
Yours faithfully,

I can quite understand, with the multitudinous duties resting upon his shoulders, how the Prime Minister was anxious to give way in matters of this kind in order to arrive at some mutual arrangement by which the difficulties could be overcome. The party who received the letter did not make it public apparently, although I understand that he acknowledged it. Shortly afterwards, when the campaign was nearing a close, he received from the private secretary of Hon. Mr. Rowell a letter as follows, a copy of which was also^ sent tto the press of the constituency:

Mr. Wesley West,
Secretary, Conservative Association, Woodstock, Ont.
Dear Sir,-
I am directed by Mr. Howell, who is in Northern Ontario, to say that before leaving for the Maritime Provinces on Sunday, Sir Robert Borden furnished Mr. Rowell with a copy of his letter to you regarding the North Oxford situation-
Sir Robert's intention was that this letter should be made public by you, and it is Sir Robert's desire that this should be done.
Yours very truly,
MAIN JOHNSON, Private Secretary.
'This letter was sent out by the private secretary of the President of the Council. The private secretary states that the Prime Minister intended that the letter should be made public. Then the private secretary evidently gives it to the press, because it is published in the papers;, that is where I first saw it. I think that in view of his connection with this matter the President of the Council should ascertain who was guilty of omitting these names from the published list.
It may be said that this circumstance did not have any effect on the election results, hut I contend that it is a remarkable coincidence-the efforts to make it impossible for this soldier at the front to get the votes of those at home who were favourable to Union Government, and also of the soldiers overseas, by omitting his name from- the records. You may say that the list was published on the 27th, and that a supplementary list was published on. the 29th. But the men overseas would naturally be anxious to know who. the candidates were; they would look over the first list, and would not take the trouble to go over the second and see whether any names had been added or omitted. The first would be the one that would receive their attention; we do not know when the second was circulated.. I am sorry indeed that I have to refer to these things in this way; it was not my intention to have done so. In the course of half a dozen words I asked a simple question, and I do not consider that I received the answer to which I was entitled. The minister may not have been responsible for the acts of this Director of Public Information at that time, but somebody was certainly responsible, and that is what I want to emphasize. I do not wish to make trouble for the Government, but I must insist upon my rights in this House and upon the right of those who are not here to see that justice is done. I submit that the guilty party in this case should be punished.

I regret exceedingly that my name has been drawn into this discussion. Ajbovie all things I always try not to appear personally in a public way any more than I can possibly help. I have nothing whatever to say against my opponent; he had as much right to run as I had. He was first the candidate of the Conservative party. My hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) said that I was nominated and brought out by the Liberal executive. It is true that I was nominated some two years ago by the Liberal party in the north riding of Oxford. In the last Parliament I took a certain position, with respect to the Military Service Bill, and when the elections were brought on last fall I called the executive of the Liberal Asociation together and made a statement to them of the position that I had taken^ in that respect. I told them that, on account of the .position I had taken, it was absolutely impossible for me to take any other course during the coming campaign than that of endorsing the Union Government. The executive of the Liberal Association were kind enough to say that they thought I had taken the proper course, and that they would endorse it and support me during the coming campaign-an offer which I very gratefully accepted. That was on Saturday. That evening the Conservative Association called a meeting of their so-called executive and pretended to accept the resignation of my opponent as Conservative candidate and to nominate him as Conservative-Unionist candidate. On Sunday afternoon they got hold of the secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association-remember, I have nothing to say against the Great War Veterans' Association, or against the great war veterans-. The member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) interrupts me. I want to tell him that it is not because he suggested anything that I say this, and we can settle it right now, or outside if he likes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I do not want any insinuations from him at all. On Sunday afternoon the Conservative clique in Woodstock got hold of the secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association-who, by the way, has never been at the front-and got him to call a meeting of his executive that afternoon and nominate my opponent as their candidate. That Sunday night the same Conservative clique in Woodstock called another meeting of their so-called executive, withdrew the resolution they had passed nominating my opponent as the Conserva-

tive-Unionist candidate, and endorsed the Great War Veterans' candidate. It was a little trickery on the part of the Conservative clique in Woodstock, that was all; and it was so recognized 'by a great many of the Conservatives in the north riding of Oxford. As to the men in France and England not knowing that my opponent was running, let me say that my opponent had been in France, had been wounded and was home. He spent six months at home canvassing against me on the pay of this Government. He was not a cripple any more than I was, . or half as much as I was, so far as that is concerned. He went back to England, not to France, and he was in England at the time the election was on. I have no doubt that he was doing the best he could for himself in England, and I do not blame him for that; that is his privilege. But I have letter after letter from men who were in France and England, saying that his name was posted on the bulletins and that they did know that he was running at the time. So I contend that those who voted for the Union Government or for me personally, as the case might be, knew that my opponent was running, and knew that he was a soldier and at that time in England.	*
Is it a fact that the hon. member ('Mr. Nesbitt) w'rote a letter to the German voters in his riding canvassing them in the election, and repudiating Union Government and the War-time Elections Act?

It is a fact that I wrote letters to some constituents in my riding, but not by any means repudiating the Unio^ Government, I was opposed to the War-time Elections Act, and I w-as opposed to it during the whole of the last session.
I would be absolutely hypocritical if I said that I was not opposed to it, because I did oppose it on the floor of* the House as energetically as I could, and everybody knows it. I may tell jthe member tfotr North Simcoe (Mr. Ourrie) that I voted for the Military Service Act, and he knows it.

The daily bulletins
sent to the troops in the field from home are very highly appreciated by all ranks, and to discontinue 'them would be an unnecessary hardship. I suggest that these bulletins should be speeded up, if anything, and that they should be delivered regularly.

I disagree with my hon. friend. I will take the case of Sir Allen
Aylesworth's son, who is in the trenches. In one issue of that sheet a cable from the President of the Council in Canada is published, with the following heading:
Sir Allen Aylesworth's son. Your Old man Has Gone Back on You.
May I ask my hon. friend the date of that?
The 27th of November.

My hon. friend knows that I stated in the House this afternoon that the publication of the Record was not transferred to my jurisdiction until January or February of this year. Until that time I had no more to do with it than my hon. friend.
My hon. friend, this afternoon, assumed the responsibility for the publication of this sheet.
I did from the time it came under any jurisdiction.
Somebody was responsible.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to this little family squabble, and I notice that some of my hon. friends are very touchy when their names are not mentioned in that Record. For instance, my hon. friend from Brantford, Mr. Cockshutt, was incensed because his1 brother's name was not published in the Record, and there is some other squabble in regard to Oxford County. Well, if my hon, friends get angry because their names are not mentioned, what about Sir Allen Aylesworth's son who is in the trenches and who sees his father's name branded as it was in that paper in which it was cabled from Canada?
Sir Allen Aylesworth's son. Your old man has gone back on you.
It tells the fake story that a sergeant said to the audience at a political meeting:
Think of it. Picture Sir Allen's son' over there in the midst of it all. See him in the trenches holding a field telephone to his ear-
A nastier way to Ihear it.
-asking why reinforcements have not come up to him, when he needs them so sorely. Then comes the answer: Aylesworth, your old- man has gone hack on you.
A ministerial, an official publication, distributed amongst our boys in the trenches'
To win the war.
Sir Allen Aylesworth, one of Canada's most prominent men, has given hds only son to fight in the trenches, and his son has to read that literature.
And we have to pay for it.

My hon. friend from
Winnipeg says: Speed up, speed up; it is too bad they do not receive this Record soon enough. I do not wish to be too per<-sonal, but I desire to nail a lie published in that sheet during tlhe last election, which was read by my son and1 forwarded to me:
Fighting officer's nomination. Hon. R. Lemie-ux's petition for rejection is discussed. Daily Record Cablegram, Quebec, Wednesday.
A despatch from Perce, Gaspe, announces that the petition of the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, for the rejection of the nomination of 'Major L. P. Gauthier, the Unionist candidate, because he is at the front, was dismissed by Judge Tessier. There will be a straight tight in this constituency between the two principal parties.
That, Mr. Chairman, is nothing 'but a lie. That 'article was sent by Canada, paid for by Canada, paid for by your humble servant as well as by my right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).
What is the date?

Oh, just in time, the 29th of November. I said this afternoon that the right hon. leader of the Opposition, who pays just as much as the Prime Minister for the publication of this sheet in England, who contributes his share as a taxpayer, had been slandered and libelled by that sheet during the whole election campaign. What do I read on November 29th?:
A victory for Sir Wilfrid Laurier, therefore, would mean that Canada would, have to drop out of the war.
This is a lie. Sir Wilfrid Laurier never appealed to his fellowmen on those lines.
Many of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's supporters have gone so far in apposition to it as to pledge themselves, if elected, to disband 100,000 men who have already been called up under the new scheme. That is to say, they have undertaken to wreck the Canadian Army Corps at the most critical moment of the war.
I am in earnest about this. Let by-gones be by-gones. Are we going to pay in the future for such literature to be distributed amongst our boys at the front? At this critical moment, when the right hon. gentleman is making a supreme appeal to this country to unite to win the war, are we going to be called upon to pay for such literature as this? You will never get united effort, national unity, if you go on with such a publication. This is- a deliberate insult to one-half of the people of Canada. The Liberals are represented as traitors', quitters, slackers, as desirous of wrecking the army. I have some confidence in my hon. friend
C'Mr. Lemieux.]
the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Roweil). I have no confidence in this Record, and much confidence as I may have in my hon. friend, I do not believe that he is a recording angel himself.

Before this very interesting debate is ended, I desire to make a few observations:	The hon. member for North
Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) stated to the House that, during the election, he did not repudiate the Union Government. I hold in my hand a letter which my hon. friend issued to his constituents in a certain section of his riding, that is, in Tavistock. I do not think he will deny this letter:
Dear Sir, I am taking the liberty of writing you to say that I would: like you to give me your support on election day, Monday the 17th, and get as many others of your neighbours to do as you can. I have, as you know, represented the Riding for the past nine years, and, I hope, satisfactorily to you all. I have been a consistent follower of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and still consider him the foremost statesman in Oanad'a.
Not a word there about the leader of the Union Government.
I have never differed with him except on one question and have been a strong opponent of the new War-time Elections Act-
That is the very Act that helped to elect him. This is the beautiful part of the letter:
-which aimed to disfranchise a certain number of my German friends, and if elected will use my best efforts to have the same repealed, as I look upon them as among our very best citizens.
That is to say, the German element in the West are our best citizens.
I also was a strong opponent of the Canadian Northern Bill, and', idf elected, will endeavour also to have that rectified.
We shall doubtless hear from him about that later on.	.
I hope, therefore, that I can count on you for your hearty support and assistance in any way you can. Hoping to hear from you favourably, I am,
Yours very truly,
E. W. Nesbitt.
That is the letter that was sent to one part of the riding. A very touching appeal was sent by the same hon. gentleman to the men in the trenches. I have not that letter here, but I have a copy of it also and no doubt it told very much in his favour over there, because he said he was in favour of the war, he was against the German element in Canada and all that kind of thing. This

is neither the time nor the place to bring up these questions, but after all is said and done, this Government has won and is in power notwithstanding those who are lukewarm behind it, and who were saying nice things about their German friends. I want to say one word in conclusion in reference to the Great War Veterans. Everybody knows that the Great War Veterans' Associations before the election, were manned largely by officers in the employ of the Government.
Any man who became president of the Great War Veterans' Association was given a job on the Hospitals Commission or something of that kind; however, the association has its heart in the right place and is probably more anxious to win the war than any other organization in this country. The action which that organization took before the election was that it would not as a body support any particular party, but would leave to local organizations perfect liberty to exercise their own judgment in selecting candidates. The Great War Veterans' Association selected candidates in a number of constituencies. They had a candidate in the Toronto riding represented by the hon. gentleman who has spoken this evening, and I might say that that is one of the strongest Tory ridings in Canada. I know, and everybody in that city knows very well, that if that gentleman had not had the en-dorsation of the Union Government and the support of the Conservative machine behind him he had no more chance of winning than a snowball. The Great War Veterans' Association opposed him simply because there was a man in the field who had served his country in the trenches, and had not gone around in clothes masquerading as a soldier, and they had a perfect right to do that. As far as I am concerned, if it is ever my duty to vote for any one in an election I am going to vote for the man who fought in the trenches, regardless of what party label he wears, and that is the right thing for those who have seen service to do in my estimation. If this war meant anything in the last election, it was
10 p.m. a call by the Government of the day to the people of this country to support the men in the trenches, and I think the action taken in Ontario in some cases smacked very much of old-time ward machine politics.
Now, about the Toronto Telegram, the widest-read journal in Ontario. The editor of that paper, a great journal-
The' CHAIRMAN: I think I must rule that out of order. What we are discussing is clause 1 of the War-Appropriation; Bill, and not the journalistic doings in the last election.

I shall endeavour to confine my remarks to the question before us, but the hon. member for Toronto has attacked the editor of the Toronto Telegram on account of his attitude in the last election, and the connection between that and the subject before us is so close that I did not think I was out of order in discussing the matter. However, I do not wish to go into any lengthy remarks, and will only say that I have noticed that the editor of the Toronto Telegram is quite capable of taking care of himself on every occasion, either on the platform or in the columns of his paper.

I do not want to interrupt this entertainment but before this act came on I was doing business with the Prime Minister. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has just read from a publication which is distributed in the trenches and paid for by the people of Canada, and he seemed to charge the President of the Privy Council with responsibility for this publication. The President of the Privy Council denied that he was responsible, and said that the publication in question was issued on 29th November, whereas he only took office as manager of the paper on 1st January. The other evening when the Prime Minister was making a statement about the appropriation for 1918-19 he seemed astonished because I took exception to certain matters in connection with the Overseas Minister of Overseas Military Forces who is three thousand miles away from us, and he invoked solidarity-II think that was>
the word, whether a minister was in France, India or China, it did not matter, as the ministers were all jointly and severally responsible for everything that happened in any department. Consequently, it seems strange to-night that the President of the Privy Council now he is confronted with the misdeeds of his confreres, should say that he did not become responsible until the 1st January, because only the otheT day we put through a Bill at the request of the Prime Minister which appointed the President of the Privy Council to his present position in the Government, dating from the month of October last. I mention this just to show how this question of solidarity works.

My hon. friend is in enor. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve said that this document emanated from the office of the President of the Council, and d said that was incorrect-as the publication had not come under my jurisdiction until a later date.
Is that the excuse that my hon. friend is making?
No, I was simply correcting my hon. friend from Maisonneuve on a statement of fact, and was saying he had not correctly stated the matter.
The statement that my hon. friend now makes is that the responsibility was thrown on him. He says he was not President of the Privy Council at that time.

I have to correct my hon. friend again. The hon. member for Maisonneuve read a statement which he said emanated from the office of the President o' the Council; as a matter of fact, he said it had been sent from that office. That was not correct, as the paper was not under my jurisdiction at that time. It was purely a question of fact I was correcting.
Under whose jurisdiction was the publication? Who was the assignor when my hon. friend became assignee of this job ?

I explained this afternoon that what is done in Canada is the telegraphing over to the other side of Canadian news. That has (been done by an officer who has served overseas, and ia now here in Canada in charge of that work.
What is his name?
Captain Wallace. He was in the Department of Militia prior to his coming under the Director of Public Information.

In what capacity
in the Department of Militia?

He was looking after
the sending over of information; I do not know whether he was directly under the Minister of Militia or not, when he was employed in connection with the Canadian War Records in the Old Country. I do not know the arrangement -under which he was operating prior to coming under the Director of Public Information.

That does not answer
my question. The hon. gentleman is in control of this publication now, or at all

events, whoever edits the paper is under his jurisdiction.	[DOT]

No. The Director of Public Information reports to me; he is an official under the charge of the President of the Council. Captain Wallace who transmits the news to this publication to England is now under the Director of Public Information. ,
And the Director of Public Information is under the jurisdiction of the President of the Council?
Yes.

I want to get this clear
in my mind, as I do not want the President of the Council shirking his responsibility.

I do not want to shirk
anything.

I want to know who
handed this Bureau of Information over to him-, and by what process it was handed over.
The Bureau of Information was not handed over. The officer in charge of this publication came from the Department of Militia, but I do not know what position he occupied in that department.

That is immaterial. The point I was making was that if solidarity should 'be invoked by the Prime Minister in one case* it should apply in every case, and the President of the Council is just as -much responsible as any other member of the 'Government for allowing these statements to go abroad.
A little more so.

Perhaps. He is a great
inspirer, I am told, and his inspiration may have filtered through to the Department of Militia; however, if this family quarrel is adjourned I will now renew my question to the Prime Minister. Does the Victory Loan of last November and all things in connection with it oome under the Department of Finance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before answering the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bureau) I would like to say one or two words in reply to certain observations made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). He seems to make a great deal out of very little. Here is an item of which he quoted only -a part in the Canadian Daily Record of November 27. It.-simply gives an -account, whioh has been published in the Canadian -press, of an incident that took

place at a political meeting at Beaverton. That is all there is about it.

That is pleasant news
for the son of Sir Allen Ayleeworth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Whether it
concerns the son of Sir Allen Ayles-worth or any one else, it is an item of public news which is -proper to be made known to the men in the trenches as it as proper to he made known to the people of Canada generally. I do not know that telegrams describing what has transpired at public meetings in Canada are to be censored from the standpoint of any individual in the trenches. I would regard that as rather an: extraordinary proposal. My hon. friend gave another quotation, in regard to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I never saw it; yet I venture to think that nothing more would be found in regard to that than I have found in regard to the item on which he lays so much stress. It has now been placed in my hands and I find it is simply an advertisement in the Canadian Daily Record publishing an article from the London Daily Mlail. It is upon these two extracts that my hon. friend would endeavour to build up a case for attacking this newspaper. I have already explained-some hon. gentlemen do not seem to understand it-that the Canadian Government does not pay out anything in connection with the Canadian Daily Record except for the news transmitted at the cost of this country overseas for the information and benefit of the men in the trenches. I do not think any hon. gentleman in this House will begrudge the very moderate expenditure of public money for enabling these men to know what is transpiring in the country they have left in order that they may fight for its continued existence.
Let no hon. gentleman imagine from what has transpired here this evening that the candidates who had served this country at the front were overlooked. I have examined the list just now and I find that about twenty men, most of whom, I am glad to say, are sitting in this House and who saw service either at the front or here in Canada or in the United Kingdom, were recognized as candidates on behalf of the Union Government at the last election.
In regard to the question which has been put to me by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), the method of procedure under the War Appropriation Act is this: it is not a vote to any particular department. I have explained this at every session of Parliament since the war began. My hon. friend has overlooked it. I have [DOT]explained it altogether about fifteen or twenty times from first to last. This is not a vote to any department of the Government; it is a vote to the Government as a whole, and therefore no portion of it can he expended by any department except under Order in Council. When any particular sum of money is appropriated to a department out of the war appropriation, that department has power to utilize those funds to that amount and no more, subject to the audit of the Auditor General and to all the precautions in regard to the expenditure of public moneys that would prevail if that particular sum of money had been voted to the department in question by Parliament in the first instance. That is the only way it can be carried out, and that is the way it is carried out. We have felt that where so large a sum of money is voted to the Government as a whole we should take rather extraordinary precautions to see that we understand the purpose for which it is to be expended, and that the accounts are properly and carefully audited. .

Lest there should be some misunderstanding in the minds of hon. gentlemen regarding the Daily Record, I will give the history of it. Early in the war it was found, as the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) has told the House', the boys were anxious for news from Canada. Accordingly we arranged to send over, I think it was one hundred wordis a day. We got a grant for one hundred words daily, and we sent that to the boys of each corps along the whole line. There was no advertising, and it was just in "flimsy." We extended it to three hundred words later, and it was under the charge of the Department of Militia and Defence. We put it under the management of two of the best newspaper men we could get-and they are all good. I may say here that the newspaper men of both political parties have played the game like gentlemen from the drop of the hat during this war, and that they have given us every legitimate assistance that they could give. One of these men was Mr. Grange and the other was Mr. Wallis. They were men who would be satisfactory to every hon. gentleman on either side of this House. We sent this news over continuously day after day,

but it was on flimsy. Later on it was printed. I do not know anything about it since that, but I think it is desirable that it should be continued, because I can back up what the hon. member from Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) said as to the great service it is to the boys at the front. They need it badly. I have no doubt it will be kept free, and that no side issues will be allowed to crawl into it.
With regard to the other question spoken of by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Bowel), I have no hesitation in saying thalt I am teetotally opposed to employing any gentleman (in the capacity of a sort of newsvendor to the ignorant people of this country, because we have none of the class that can be moved by iany such process as that. It is nothing buit an insult to the intelligence of the people of Canada foT a lot of these fellows to go around preaching to the people, telling them to do this, and to do that, and to read Napoleon. The selection of a man who has shown himself so prejudiced and so unworthy of public confidence as this gentleman who has been selected by the President of the Privy Council, is a mistake of the first magnitude. As to the others in the department, I know nothing concerning them at all. They .may be all right or all wrong. But if they belong to the type I have indicated, all I *can say is that I have never yet seen men of that type do anything to build up the country. As far -as I am concerned, I am totally opposed to the action of the President of the Privy Council in establishing this department at considerable expense to the country. I have no hesitation in saying-(and my belief has not been changed in the slightest degree by anything that has been said to-day-that the organization of that department composed of these gentlemen, has not for its object the education of the people along lines connected with the winning of the war, but has for its object the education of the people along the lines that will be convenient for certain gentlemen in case they want to use them politically later on.

In regard to the history of this sheet, the Canadian Daily Record, at one time overseas, I received that paper, or rather a collection of typewritten sheets, which I read with considerable pleasure. Because, after all, the home papers arrive, as a rule, two ot three weeks late. This sheet, I understand, was instituted at the time that my hon. friend, the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) was in charge, and consisted of about one hundred words.

tSir SAM HUGHES: It was suggested by the notorious character, Max Aitken, Lord Beaverbrook, who had the .interests of the beys at heart then the same as now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Was not the article which the hon. gentleman first read an advertisement?
It was an advertisement and I stated it to be such.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not understand the hon. gentleman to say that.

We have never had any statement as to whether any moneys have been turned in to the Canadian Government, or to the Canadian War Record Office, for advertisements printed in this paper during the period of the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As a matter of fact the Canadian Government does not expend any money upon the publication of the Canadian War Record at all. The only money that it does expend is in sending telegraphic news messages, and, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman has said as to the character of the paper I am under the impression that he has not made a very careful study of its columns, or he would not have committed himself quite so absolutely as he did. For example on the very page from which my hon. friend, the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) quoted I find this:
Denies all knowledge.
Sir Wilfrid makes reply to Premier on recruiting.
(Daily Record Cablegram.)
Ottawa, Monday.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier has issued a statement replying to the Premier's speech at Sydney, when Sir Robert said he had asked the Opposition to co-operate in regard to recruiting.
In his reply, Sir Wilfrid Laurier says he has no knowledge whatever of these invitations.
A correction, according to Sir Wilfrid Laurier's. ideas, of a statement I had made at Sydney. I would suppose that any hon.. gentleman looking at a page of the paper-

Would the Prime Minister like to have a photograph of that paragraph, as well as of the paper, shown to anybody in this House? If a photograph were taken of it it would surely be shown that it was an imputation with respect to the honesty of the right hon. leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I must confess that I can hardly enter into the state of mind which would attribute any such imputation as that to the article that I have just read. I shall not discuss it; hon. gentlemen can see it for themselves, as they have heard it for themselves. According to my limited powers of understanding, I should say it could not by any possibility whatever convey any such imputation as the hon. gentleman has mentioned.

The Prime Minister said just now that we should not begrudge the money we are spending for that publica-

tion. It is the same old game. When we get up, and there has been a family quarrel, I am surprised that they do not yell " Quebec." We on this side of the House do not begrudge any expenditure foT the soldiers. If you want to have unity, and have us join hands with you in everything, it is high time that these imputations should stop, and when anybody on the other side is in a hole it is sufficient that he cry out: " Oh, well, you have to cry, because this is an expenditure for war purposes." Nobody on the other side can complain that we have embarrassed the Government in any way since the beginning of the session, even when they brought in bad measures, or measures that would be obnoxious to any man who desired to keep this a democratic country if it was not a time of war. We do not want to have any trouble, and it is for that reason that'we object to these imputations that have been made against us for the last year or more. As my hon. friend has said, the Canadian Daily Record has contained some shameful posters and literature, which was published in the Ontario- papers, and the title " Union Publication Committee," telephone such a number, and such an address, appeared on the sheet. Now, I have no objection to sending this publication to the trenches. The Prime Minister says it does not cost a cent to send it. I say go on and spend money on it, and let the boys in the trenches know what is going on in this country. It is not the spending of $200 more a week or a month that will cripple this country. The object is to keep them in contact with their people. I suppose its not costing the public anything is the excuse for making it a political sheet to be sent to the trenches. We are onto the game, and we won't stand for it, and are determined that these imputations shall go on no longer. The Prime Minister told me that this amount of $500,000,000 is appropriated to the Government as a whole. That being so, I want to see the report of the whole Government as to that Victory Loan. The reason is this: On page 597 of unrevised Hansard, the Prime Minister made the statement that the war expenditure for the Finance Department for the fiscal year 1914-15 was $149,630.09; in 1915-16, $72,000; in 1916-17, $54,000; in 1917-18, $6,000. Now, before 31st March last, the Victory Loan was floated, and my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) told us- the other 
night that the cost of floating that loan was about three millions of dollars.
Five millions.

And might increase to five millions. My hon. friend is here to correct me. He said that the cost so far was about three millions, but that when all his friends were satisfied it would amount to five millions. I Would like to know from the Prime Minister where this five millions representing the commission paid for the raising of the Victory Loan of $300,000,000 is going to be charged.
And the advertising.

I thought I understood that covered all the expenditure incurred in the raising of the Victory Loan.
Mr. A. K. MlAGLEAiN:	On the occasion
to which my hon. friend refers, I gave to the House all the information that was available in connection with the cost of the last Victory 'Loan. The expenditures in that connection, so far as known, amount to $3,620,395. But I said there were additional expenditures to be accounted for, and I am very sorry they are not yet available. But they will be available in a few days when 'I shall be able to lay on the table of the House a complete statement of the expenditure. It will approximate nearly five million dollars, but the total cost of the loan will amount to one and one-quarter per cent, which is an exceedingly low rate.

I am not criticising that; I did not rise in a spirit of criticism. I wanted to find out how it is that, according to the Prime Minister's statement, the expenditure for the Finance Department for the fiscal year 1917-18 is $6,024.02, when we know that the floating of this loan is costing the country over four million dollars.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think that has . any connection with the loan. I am not very familiar with the administration of the Department of Finance but my impression is that, with respect to all loans floated in this country, the cost is deducted from the proceeds of the loan. Perhaps the Acting Minister of Finance can say if that is the case?
(Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That has been the practice, I think, in the past. My hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queens can give the House more information on that point than I can. [DOT]

'Mr. FIELDING:	I have not followed
the argument just now. Speaking generally, the hon. gentleman's statement of practice is correct.

I would like to
afford the information that the hon. gentleman desires, if I o.an give it to him.
I did not understand his question. Would he repeat it?

The Department of Finance has raised a loan of $500,000,000, if I understand it aright, iby means of a Victory Loan from the people. This loan has cost a certain amount to the country. My method of keeping books would be to charge the cost of that loan somewhere. Now, if you are going to ;pay $5,000,000, you won't get $500,000,000; you will only get $495,000,000. I understand from the Prime Minister that the country will be credited ith only $495,000,000, is that correct?

$398,000,000 is
the proceeds of the loan.
M.r. BUREAU:	I am using $500,000,000
for the sake of argument. There is a discrepancy in the amount realized of $5,000,000. There has been realized1 from the loan $495,000,000 and there have actually been issued bonds or certificates to the amount of $500,000,000. Am I correct in that statement?
Yes, hut what is wrong about it?

Nothing is wrong with
*it. But if the Finance Department have been handling this loan, where is the cost of floating it shown? The Prime Minister says that this is a loan which is made to the Government as a whole. Is it distributed' among the various departments? Do I understand that the Militia Department, for instance, get $200,000,000?

My hon. friend
misunderstood the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was talking
about the appropriation, not about the loan.

All war appropriations are made on behalf of the Government. Ordinarily our estimates appropriate money to the different departments for different purposes, and each department has control over the money voted. But in the case of war expenditures, the appropriation is made by the Government, and the Government is responsible, not the department actually making the expenditure. I informed the House the
other day as fully as I could of the exact cost of the Victory Loan. I am sorry that complete and exact details of the expenditure are not available; I hope, however, that they will be available next week, when I shall lay them on the Table. The Victory Loan was in charge of a committee whose headquarters were at Toronto, and the expenditures were incurred by that committee. We must Tely upon them to submit all the details to the Department of Finance. We are promised the particulars this ' week.
That will be in the public accounts?
The cost of the loan will be deducted from the proceeds of the sale of the bonds.
There will be that discrepancy between the two sides of the books.
The hooks of the department will show the total receipts and the total cost of making the loan.
The hon. gentleman said that there was a committee in Toronto. What committee was that?
Some members of the committee were from Montreal and other parts of Canada, I believe. I am sorry that I cannot inform my hon. friend as to the membership of the committee.
Will my hon. friend get that information?
Yes.
In the return which my hon. friend promises to bring down, will he give details of the various items of expenditure under the different headings- newspaper advertising, and so on?
The information I propose to lay on the Table will disclose the exact amount paid for publicity, and the amount paid to each newspaper in Canada.

Will it contain the
amount paid for publicity through the newspapers as distinguished from publicity through other means?
Yes.

I listened with great
attention to the statement made by the President of the Council this afternoon with regard to his scheme of propaganda throughout Canada and his explanation of the publication in different books and maga-

zines of the reasons for the war and the aims of the Allies. I was not, however, in any way convinced that this country ought to spend so large an amount as the cost of the scheme proposed by the President of the Council would involve. I submit that if the press, not only of the province of Quebec but of all the other provinces as well, were allowed to state exactly the views of the people of the country the people would be thoroughly acquainted with our aims in this war and the objects which we wish to attain. The President of the Council told us that he had appointed as head of the Bureau of Public Information a gentleman by the name of Nichols. I do not wish to repeat what the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) said, but if what he said is true-and it has not been contradicted either by the President of the Council or by any member on the other side-Mr. Nichols certainly is not competent to be placed in such a position as that which has been assigned to him by the minister. Mr. Nichols edited two newspapers in Montreal; what happened to those newspapers? Well, they attacked the exMinister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) for what purpose I do not know.
I know, though.
The ex-Minister of Militia thinks he knows. I hope that after I have finished these few remarks, he will explain why he knows.
I did.

Might I correct the hon. member? It was assumed -by Canadians-, the Canadian High Commissioner and others, that we had nothing to say in the matter. When- I laid the matter before the British Government, 1 did so- very clearly, and Viscount Kitchener, Sir Douglas Haig, Sir William Robertson, Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Bon-ar Law and others recognized our position exactly as I laid it down.

I understand from what the hon. member s-ays that our official representative in England, our High Commissioner at London, was under the impression that we had absolutely nothing to do with the conduct of our army the moment it landed in England?
Yes.
Our Minister of Militia at that time maintained the contrary. What was the result? The Commissioner is still there, and the minister is out.
Happy, though.

Happy to be out. Maybe the ex-minister is happy, but if the exminister contended for the maintenance of our autonomy, I may say that I am not happy that he is out, because the stand taken by him is the stand that should be taken by every true and sincere Canadian. We are subjects of the British Empire, it is true. I would be the last man- to- forget th-at I am a British subject; I would be the last man to preach, in my province or in my constituency any disloyalty towards the British Crown; but on the other hand, I would be the last man to say that I am the slave of England or of Downing street.
What about the American forces in England and France at the present time?

The American forces have been placed by their Government at the disposal of General Foch as Commander-inChief of the Allied forces, but our Government never had anything to do as to our
troops once they went overseas. That is the difference.
I was astounded, I was amazed this afternoon when the Minister of Militia declared that he did not even know who was the army commander of the Canadian corps at present. Where do we stand? We are no longer in 1760. We are no longer at the stage when this Canada of ours was merely a small colony which a few thousands of people were trying to open up to colonization and civilization. This Canada -is a country and the Canadian people are a nation. We are not a Crown colony. What is our status? When you take a country like Montenegro, which has contributed to the Allied forces in this war a force of about 10,000 men, whenever there is a military conference in Paris or in London the representatives of Montenegro are called in to give their opinion. And at such conferences, where is our -Canadian representative? When England decided to declare war on Germany and Austria, was the Prime Minister of this country consulted? Did the Prime Minister of this country receive a cable from the Imperial authorities? If he did, I should like him to let me know. We were not consulted as to the declaration of war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may tell the hon. gentleman that we were in constant communication with the Imperial authorities for days -before war broke out.

Constant communication with the Imperial authorities possibly, but if the Prime Minister wants to be sincere he will admit he never was consulted as to whether this Empire -should declare war on Germany or not.

This Parliament did take action.
Mr. 'CANNON: It was never consulted as to the declaration of war.
The hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about.

I know what I am talking -about.
Mr. CLfRRIE: No, you do not.
I 'do not wish to carry on a discussion with the hon. member along these lines. Ignorance is no argument, and he can keep his to himself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I think that a great deal of useless discussion would be avoided if the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), who now has the floor, would

bring his remarks a little nearer to the Bill under consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: " This Act may be cited as The War Appropriation Act, 1918."
