speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is that we are discussing the short title of this Bill, and that the remarks now being made by the hon. member for Dorchester are not in order, *as they do not relate to the clause now under discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Once again,
and for the last time, I call the hon. gentleman to order. He is now discussing the principle of this Bill-discussion which might more properly have taken place on the second reading. In any event, it certainly is not in order on the clause under consideration,
With all respect for the Chairman of this committee I wish to

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order.
Mr. 'CANNON:	On the second reading
of this Bill it was distinctly understood-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
May I ask the Prime Minister if it was not distinctly understood that we could discuss the principle of the Bill in committee just as on the second reading?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not so understand.
There was something of that kind understood.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We will look
it up and see what it was. I remember that I said I would give a great deal of information in committee which I might otherwise have given on the second reading.

The Bill was given its
second reading to rush matters, but on the distinct understanding that we could discuss its principle in committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not aware of that.

That is what we gathered'
from the Prime Minister's remarks the other day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: I bow to your decision. The honourable the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) this afternoon gave us a statement as to the great scheme he had to open up the minds of the people of Canada as to the object of the country in this war. If we are to believe the remarks made by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and which were not contradicted, if the Government wish to carry on a propaganda of the same character as that which was carried on in England during the election and if the Liberals of Canada are to be represented in these official papers as the Kaiser's friends I do not think it would be fair for any gentleman on the other side of the Hbuse, not even for the President of the Privy Council, to ask us to pay for papers that are libelling us all the time. The President of the Privy Council says that his sole object is to unite the population of this country and to increase our strength in fighting Germany. As far as that is concerned, we are always unanimous.
In theory.
In theory and in practice.
Not to any alarming extent.

We may differ as to means ' and methods but I think our spirit is the same. I think that our ideas are in common and that on both sides we wish to win the war and to prosecute it with the greatest possible vigour. I was saying, Mr. Chairman, that this propaganda that is being carried on has certain dangers. Why should the people of this country who are divided in their political views be called
upon to pay the expenses of publications, lectures and meetings when the views expressed in these publications, lectures and meetings may not be in the interest of unity or of the country generally? As far as the President 'of the Privy Council is concerned, I have not the pleasure or the honour of knowing him personally, but I have known him casually through reports published in the papers and through speeches made in the House.
Oh, oh.

If any hon. member wishes to interrupt me I would ask him to rise. These publications may be good, but judging by those which have been issued in the past, I do not think it would be fair or just to the people of this country to ask them to pay for them. In England, in France, and among our overseas troops, these publications have been issued absolutely for political purposes. If the Unionist party wishes to promote its aims and to improve its chances of being elected, should1 not the Unionist party pay its party and election expenses instead of the Government bearing these expenses? It is not fair, just or equitable. I notice in memorandum No. 3, which is being distributed to the members, a statement published on page 60. This statement contains one item to which I wish to call the attention of the right hon. the Prime Minister. It is an item as to the Ross rifles. According to that statement, we have spent $8,360,358.32 for the period covered by the memorandum. What has become of those Ross rifles? The ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam. Hughes), I understand, was a firm supporter of the Ross rifle. He was a very convinced believer in the qualities of the Ross rifle as a war weapon. Last year, without any warning, the workers who were employed at the Ross rifle factory in Quebec received notice that their services were no longer required.

Does the hon. gentleman know if there is any truth in the rumour that for the purpose of carrying on the war they are trying to manufacture a *annon in Quebec that will shoot three thousand miles?
APr. OANNpN:	I do not know if such
a gun is to be manufactured, but if it were I think it would be very useful to the hon. member because he does not fire very far.
Will the hon. gentleman undertake to raise a battalion to operate such, a gun from his constituency?

The hon. member may think he is very funny. If he is of that opinion I am not going to disabuse his mind of the idea, because when a man wishes to be funny I like him to enjoy his own jokes. But 1 wish to tell the hon. gentleman that we on this side are not here to make jokes. We are not here to laugh, but to discuss as seriously as we can the problems -which are submitted to us, and we are thoroughly in earnest in our resolution to do so. If the hon. member does not agree with me I am very sorry for him. I do not wish to be funny, I desire to be serious and I hope he will adopt the same attitude. I was remarking to the Prime Minister that the Ross rifle factory in Quebec is closed. The closing of that factory was a real calamity, because it deprived thousands of labourers of employment and forced them to leave our city and to go elsewhere to seek for work. I would like , the Government to give us an explanation as to why the Ross rifle factory was closed, because the explanations offered by the Government at the time were incomplete and unsatisfactory. The people of Quebec are asking why that factory should have been closed after the Government had made such a large expenditure as they did. in connection with the manufacture and purchase of Ross rifles. I will not take up time in unduly discussing this matter, but I sincerely hope that the Government, before this discussion closes, will vouchsafe a satisfactory answer on the subject.

If the hon. gentleman would apply to the former member for Edmonton. Mr. Oliver, he would get all the information possible on that subject.
Mr. CANNON": That is indeed a very bright suggestion on the hon. gentleman's part.
May I inquire if the military publication known as "Knouts and Lashes" is published by the department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I never heard of it before.
Does the Government grant any subvention to that publication?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not that I am aware of.

This afternoon I asked for some information from the Prime Minister as to the management of the Department

of Militia Overseas. I did not want at the time to interrupt the trend of the discussion that was immediately afterwards started' by other speakers on other subjects, and which served to divert attention from the point which I raised, but I now wish to press for an answer, because the point involved is most important. If we wish to continue to consider ourselves as a nation we must deal with our army as a nation does. The Prime Minister told us that in the direction of military operations the Canadian commander in the field had to receive orders from the Commander in Chief of the Allied Armies. In that arrangement we all concur, but in our expeditionary force there are regiments, brigades, divisions and army corps. We have staffs for the regiments, and also brigade and division and army staffs, and we have the army council advising the Minister of Militia Overseas. But it seems to me, and the same idea occurs to a great many members of this House as well as to a large number of our people, that such being the case, promotions in and appointments to the Canadian Expeditionary Force could be easily followed, could be easily recommended, and easily kept under the control of the Minister of Militia Overseas, who should be required to report these matters to the Canadian Government for the information of the House. If I understood the Prime Minister correctly, he told us that the military operations were under the control of the War Office and the Commander in Chief of the Allied Armies, but he did not advise us as to how the appointments or promotions in the regiments, or on the brigade, division and army corps staffs were made. Neither did he answer the other question I asked, which was whether the commander of our army in the field reports	either to	the Minister ofMilitia Overseas, or directly to the Government, how our troops are ordered into action and how they	come	out.	Thisinformation I also deem to be of importance. Field	Marshall	Haig,	the	commander of the British troops in the field, now acts under the supreme command of General	Foch,	but	that
does not prevent the former from sending despatches to his Government as to how the troops go into action and how they come out. I, therefore, wish for informationxon those points: First, as to the appointment of officers and as to their displacement; secondly, as to the orders given to our troops to go into action or to come out of it, and whether the commander in the field

has any orders to report to the Government by despatches in that respect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have already explained, and I am sorry the hon. gentleman did not grasp my statement, that in so far as appointments and promotions at the front are concerned, they are carried out practically by the military commanders in the brigades, the divisions and the army corps. We do not interfere at all, and I think the public would regard us as practically insane if we did in this instance attempt to do so. In the case of the higher commands word is sent to us, but naturally we feel that those who are in command of the troops understand better the qualifications, the experience and the ability of the men selected for a particular post.
Who appoints the higher commands?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In the case of a brigade, there would be a recommendation from the commander which would, I presume, require the approval of the divisional commander and the commander of the corps. In the case of a division, the divisional commander would make his recommendation to the commander of the corps. It all goes in that way. Inasmuch as the commander of the corps is responsible in the last analysis, why, naturally his approval must be secured. And then in the case of important commands-

We cannot hear a
word.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was saying
that the commander of the corps must approve, as I understand, because he is, in the highest degree, responsible. As to important commands, we have been consulted over here. But we have never attempted to over-ride the recommendations made from the front.

While what the
Prime Minister says in practice may be true, surely the Prime Minister does not for a second dispute that he and his Cabinet have the final say in the appointment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Absolutely, we
have, and I have said so repeatedly.
It is quite possible for a gentleman living in Otta-wa to know quite as much about the capacity of these officers as a gentleman thirty miles in the rear of the fighting line.	*

I would like to ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of
Militia if French-speaking recruits will be sent to the trenches as a unit; that is, will they be merged into French regiments like the 22nd Battalion? I understand that the 150th Regiment was broken up in England. It was commanded by Colonel Barre, a good officer, who has received the medal of the Legion d'Honneur.
I want to impress upon the Minister of Militia that in my judgment it is important that French Canadians should be kept together. Last week the minister said that he regretted very much that owing to the necessities of the situation a certain regiment which came from a certain province had to be disbanded, and that it would have been better for the spirit of the corps if it had remained together. I think that special steps should be taken to see that French Canadians, a great number of whom do not understand English, shall be commanded by officers who can speak French. Sometimes orders may be given of extreme importance, and it would seem to me that these instructions should be given by officers who can give the necessary explanation in their language. I would strongly and energetically urge that French Canadians should not be merged with English regiments, because they will have sufficient hardships to endure without the added difficulty of language.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

I am just finishing; I won't be long. I noticed in a Montreal paper a statement by Colonel Mignault, who has been to the front, and is, I presume, well known to the Militia Department, in which he argues along this line, that the French Canadians should be kept together as a unit.
Major-General MEWBURN: I think I said some days ago in the House that the whole organization is on the territorial principle, that in England they have some regiments linked up with those overseas. Any recruits coming from Military Districts No. 4 and No. 5, taking in Montreal and Quebec, go over and are put into the reserve battalions, and from these they are gradually sent over as reinforcements to the units in the fighting line coming from their home districts. There- are several regiments at the front known as Quebec regiments. I won't say that they are filled completely with French Canadians, because, I think, in some instances, that they were unable to keep up their reinforcements. But the I3th, 14th, 22nd, 24th, 5th, and the 87th are all known as Quebec regi-

ments coming from the province of Quebec, and the reserve units in England take care of these men, and they go from there to the line regiments in the front.

Will the hon. minister promise the House to put himself into communication with the Imperial authorities to see that French Canadians shall be kept together as much as possible? It is not an evasive answer that I wish to have.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Probably the Minister of Militia would allow me to answer the hon. gentleman's question. We all know that the 22nd Battalion, which has covered itself with so much glory at the front, is entirely a French Canadian battalion.
Not entirely.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: II think so. As the French Canadians go from Montreal to England and as the Minister of Militia has pointed out, they are put into what is known in England as the 10th Reserve Battalion under Colonel DesRbsiers. They are all French Canadians there; I was in that camp and saw them. So I wish to assure my hon. friend that the French Canadians at the front are kept together ir*. the 22nd Battalion and officered by French Canadians.

The right hon. Prime Minister answered the first question. He will perhaps be able to -tell me whether the Government received any despatch from the commander of the troops in the field as to how they were ordered into action, and how they came out?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Officer Commanding the corps in the field reports to us through the Minister of the Overseas Service. We receive very frequent reports. As far as ordering them into action or out of action is concerned, of course, the Government sitting here, in Ottawa has nothing to do with ordering them into action any more than the people in the War Office have to do with directing General's Haig's movements. These things must be done by the military commanders at the front.
My right hon. fnend said a minute ago that before the war broke out the Government was in constant consultation-

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I want to call your attention to the fact that speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly rele-
[Major-General Mewburn.]
vant to the item under consideration. It seems to me that hon. gentlemen opposite have flagrantly violated that rule this evening.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With the unanimous consent of the committee, and also of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia, it was understood that all questions relating to the administration of the forces and all expenditures connected with this Bill should be discussed in committee. I do not think that the hon. member has wandered far enough away from that aspect of the matter under consideration to warrant my calling him to order.

I assure my hon. friend that I do not want to delay the procedure unnecessarily. I simply wish to obtain from the Prime Minister such information as will enable us to appreciate how things are managed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For about a week, or perhaps more, before the war broke out the Government of the United Kingdom were in constant communication with us. I was away from Ottawa-I left, I think, on 23rd July-and these communications, the purport of which was transmitted to me, were of such a character that on July 30th I came to the conclusion that I should return to Ottawa. I arrived on the morning of August 1st, and went over the communications which had been received. A great many more came during the next three or four days, until war broke out. We were kept constantly advised. On 1st August I took upon myself the responsibility of advising the Government of the United Kingdom that if war did unfortunately break out. this country would stand with the Mother 'Country and the other dominions of the Empire to the end. I further sent them a confidential telegram, which has since been made public, stating that I believed we could send a division over almost immediately. -The question whether or not Parliament and the country would stand behind that declaration came up in the first instance at the session of Parliament which opened on 18th August. On that occasion this country, through the representatives of the people in Parliament assembled, decided that the course which I bad taken was the proper one and they would stand behind it without a dissenting voice.

The Prime Minister has left out a very important point-

that Britain did not ask Canada to support her. The action of Canada was purely voluntary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I certainly desired to be so understood. The telegram which I sent on 1st August was not in response to any appeal; it was a voluntary offer which I made on behalf of the people of Canada, and which was afterwards ratified by this Parliament.

;I asked for this information because I understood the Prime Minister to inform the member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) that for over-a week before the war broke out he had been in constant consultation with the Imperial Government. I gather from what the Prime Minister says that the Government was in constant consultation 'with the Imperial authorities so far as our participation in the war was concerned, but not so far as the declaration of war itself was concerned.
Last year the Ross rifle factory was closed down. I was not in the House at the time, but I understood from a declaration made [DOT]by the acting Prime Minister of that time, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) that the Ross rifle factory had been closed down on account of the rifle having been discarded, and that the Ross rifle factory would be transformed into a factory for the manufacture of Lee-Enfield rifles. What has been done with the Ross rifle factory, and what steps have been taken to convert it into a Lee-Enfield rifle factory?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No arrangements have been made to convert the Ross rifle into Lee-Enfield rifle. Speaking without any expert knowledge, I doubt very much whether that would be possible. The troops were being armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle, and it was not considered desirable to proceed with the manufacture of more Ross rifles. The best disposition possible was made of those on hand.

What has been done with the machinery that was in the Ross rifle factory?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Some parts
of the machinery that were non required for the manufacture of rifles have been sold; I could not give the exact quantity. I understand it is not the intention of the Government to continue the manufacture of Ross rifles. Some scraps of machinery and material that were not further required have been sold.
Mr. LAViIGUEUR:	At what price was
the Ross rifle factory appropriated by the Government?
Major-General MEWBURN: An Order in Council fixed a maximum price on the expropriation of $3,000,000.
Is it the intention of the Government to manufacture Lee-Enfield rifles in the Roes rifle factory?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We had a great deal of correspondence with the British Government as to what rifle would eventually be used throughout the Empire. It was recognized at the Imperial War Conference, that it was desirable 'that all troops of the Empire should be equipped and armed, as far as possible, in the same way. It is still quite uncertain what type of rifle will eventually be used. One 'thing is certain: that at the end of this war there will be a very much greater stock of rifles on hand than the Empire will require for peace purposes. Under these circumstances i't is obvious that we coiuild come to no con-elusion as to the manufacture of any particular type of rifle in this country in tile immediate future.

Is there any proposal to turn the Rose rifle factory into a plant for the manufacture of machine guns for a foreign Government?
Major-General MEWBURN:	There was
a suggestion in that regard, and some negotiations took place, but nothing came of them.
Are the details of expenditure in connection with the expropriation of the Ross rifle factory published officially?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are available in statements that have been made in the Houee.
I do not think any statement was laid on the Table so far as the expenditure incurred is concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was in the memorandum alluded to a statement as to the expenditure during that particular year.

I understand the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) told us the other day that he expected the fourth volume of the Auditor General's Report to be available in a few days, or, at least, that he could tell us shortly when it would be available. Can the minister tell us now when we may expect the fourth volume which contains a great deal of information and details as to the expenditure? Tho House will not find our inquiries too ex-



tended or obnoxious, because $500,000,000 was voted last year and have been expended, and as insufficient reports have been laid on the Table of the House, I think our inquiry is justified.

I quite agree that the hon. gentleman's demands are proper. I am sorry I cannot give him any further information this evening, but I shall do so to-morrow afternoon.
Mr. JOS. READ: I just want to draw the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to the very great danger to which they have been exposing the Empire by not sticking to the truth, especially in those publications. Take for instance, that publication that is still under discussion. In that sheet which my hon. friends had circulating amongst our boys, it was stated that if Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the right hon. leader of the Opposition, won the election, it would mean that Canada intended to quit. Did ever any hon. gentleman opposite think of what moral effect such a statement would produce not only upon our boys at the front, but upon the Imperial forces? Supposing Sir Wilfrid Laurier had won the election, what a state those people would have been in. Hon. members opposite must remember that the morale of an army is of as much importance as its ability to fight, and yet at the risk of lowering the morale of our army, my hon. friends, in order to win the election, go to the extreme method of publishing an absolute falsehood. My hon. friends want to be careful what they do.

I would suggest to the Prime Minister that in view of the fact that we have not the fourth volume of the Auditor General's Report, and in view of the fact that the report of the Military Service Council was distributed only to-day, the consideration of the clause under discussion should be postponed until another day, and that the committee should rise and report progress. There is not immediate urgency, and we shall not by any means unfairly delay the discussion of these matters, but it is only fair that, before the title of the Bill is carried, we should he put in possession of the documents and details.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not quite see the relevancy of the report of the Military Service Council to the appropriation under discussion. The report of the Militia Council, I am informed, was laid upon the table of the House about a week ago. Perhaps my hon. friend is confusing the one with the other. There are

two distinct reports. One is the report of the Militia Council, which does contain a great deal of information relative to the appropriation that is now being asked for. The other is the report of the Military Service Council, an absolutely different thing, which has to do with the enforcement of the Military Service Act. According to my apprehension, that has very little relation to the appropriation that is now being asked for. I was not aware that the fourth volume of the Auditor General's Report -was not brought down. If the fourth volume contains his report respecting the Department of Militia and Defence, that, of course, is very relevant to the subject under discussion.
It contains all the expenditure overseas, and especially the latest expenditure. The expenditure made by the Military Service Council comes under the War Appropriation Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I know it does,
but the report deals with methods, not with expenditures, and therefore, notwithstanding the suggestion of my hon. friend, I venture to impress upon him that it really has very little relation to this appropriation. The other two reports which he has mentioned have very direct relation to the appropriation.

In view of the fact that the fourth volume of the Auditor General's Report, containing important details and information, is not available, I would suggest that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We had better pass this section. We have been at it for two days, and as it consists of only one line, if we should take as much time for every other line in the Bill, we would get through with this appropriation by next September. I hope we shall get through a little earlier than that. I should like to say further that when my hon. friend suggests there is not some urgency about this matter, he is not thoroughly well advised. Since the 31st day of March, we have not had any money to carry on this war, and while it is perfectly true, I suppose, that bills and accounts have not yet come in to any great extent, we may expect them to come in very soon, and until this measure is passed, there will be no money with which to meet them. Therefore, while I do not desire in any way to restrict discussion, but rather to invite it, I hope hon. gentlemen will not be under the impression that there is no urgency in connection with this measure.

Will the Minister of Militia be good enough to tell the committee what procedure must be taken to enter the Royal Fiying Corps?
Major-General MEWBURN: Applications are made to the Officer Commanding the Royal Flying Corps in the Royal Bank Building, Toronto. General Hoare is the Officer Commanding, and when he is travelling between Texas and the Canadian camps, applications may be made to. the Officer Commanding the Royal Flying Corps at Toronto, where the headquarters is.

My reason for mentioning this matter to the minister is that I have had occasion to hear of a couple of cases of young men in the city of Quebec who wanted to apply for a commission in* that particular corps and who were not able to succeed for one reason or another. The men are fully qualified in the way of education, physical capacity and so on.
Major-General MEWBURN: The Royal Flying Corps is not under our jurisdiction; it is under the Imperial War Department. They have their head office at Toronto. They have several camps in this country; they will be opening up at Camp Borden next month or probably the end of this month. If the hon. member finds any difficulty in getting information, I shall be glad to give him all information possible.

Has the minister nothing tc do with the corps?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Nothing
whatever. The appointments are all made through the officers of the Flying Corps around here.

To my personal knowledge the -branch of the Aviation Corps in Montreal is- under the charge of Mr. Light-all, and he has done excellent work in Montreal. I have sent many young men to him myself, and after examination at his office, where an Imperial officer is present, these young men are enlisted. I was surprised to see how rapidly it could be done.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I presume
my hon. friend is referring to young men who want a commission in the Flying Corps. The Flying Corps have offices all over the country-in Montreal, in the West, and in. the United States-and applications are received through any of these offices. I was speaking of the headquarters of the Flying Corps in Toronto.
59J

I would suggest that the minister get some of his officers to ascertain just where these offices are, and have the information published in the newspapers so that these young men would know where to apply.
Major-General MEWBURN:	We pass
these applications right along.
Let the newspapers publish the information so the boys will have the data.

I think the minister said the Government had nothing to do with the Royal Flying Corps, but I find on page- 61 of Memorandum No. 3 that the flying officers are paid at the rate of ?6-I do not know whether that is per day or not-and an allowance. Apparently this money is paid by the country, so the Government must have something to do with the Royal Flying Corps.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman probably did not hear the explanation which I made. There was some allowance made by this country to officers who went into the Flying Corps and lost pay on that account.

My only object in bringing forward this matter is to facilitate the enlisting of men in the Flying Corps. For some reason at the present time there is a great deal of red tape to. be gone through. I think if the minister would look into this matter it would help considerably.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I shall do
so with pleasure. I know the Flying Corps are only too glad to get recruits, and I am surprised to hear there is any red tape in the matter. .
I asked the Prime Minister some time ago to state the reasons why the Ross rifle factory was closed. I do not know whether he forgot about the subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I certainly could not have forgotten about it, because I gave the reasons, but .perhaps my hon. friend did not hear them. I explained that the Ross rifle was not now used, that the men were armed with another rifle, and therefore it would not be in the public interest to continue manufacturing the .Ross rifle.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before passing clause 1, I should like to remind the committee that it w.as on this clause that all these questions concerning expenditure were asked. If any hon. members have any

further questions of that nature to ask, I think it would be a proper time to ask for the information before this clause passes.
I understood from the Prime Minister's statement that further questions could be asked when the full volume of the Auditor . General's Report was available.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let me relieve my hon. friend's anxiety -at once. If the Chairman has no objection, I see no reason why we should not continue this discussion, in so far as it is relevant, on any other clause of the Bill. There is no reason why information could not be given on any other clause. But I hope it will not be found necessary to have a discussion of quite so comprehensive a scope on the other clauses. I would suggest that the discussion be a little more relevant, but so far as relevant information is concerned, there will not be the slightest objection to giving it on any clause of the Bill, or even on the preamble, which we have not yet reached.
The Prime Minister will render us this justice: That so far as relevancy is concerned, this side of the House has kept to the point as closely as hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was not intending to draw any comparison whatever.

Section agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden the House adjourned at 12 midnight.
Friday, April 19, 1918.
